rows.question: My mother is behaviour really falls in your chest i'm in out hard, and she is confused and hot to touch.
rows.answer:
**If your mother is struggling to breathe, breathing very fast or hard, or is hard to wake, please call 111 now.** Confusion together with a high temperature and laboured breathing can point to a serious infection, such as a chest infection (pneumonia), which can come on quickly in older people and needs urgent medical attention. If you're unsure whether it's that serious, you can call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, nurse advice), but if your instinct says something is badly wrong, trust it and ring 111.

While you wait for help, sit her upright if she's comfortable, keep calm and stay with her. Loosen heavy clothing or blankets, and offer small sips of water only if she's alert enough to swallow safely. Speak slowly and reassuringly, since confusion and fever can be very frightening for her. If you can, have her medication list and any recent health changes ready for the ambulance crew.

A sudden change in confusion or behaviour in someone with dementia is very often caused by a treatable physical problem, like a chest or urinary infection, rather than the dementia itself [S5]. That's why getting her checked promptly matters so much. It's not your fault if this came on quickly, and you're doing the right thing by paying attention.

This sounds frightening and exhausting. Once she's being cared for, if you need someone to talk to, you can call or text 1737 any time, or ring the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001. Are you with her now, and is she breathing comfortably?

rows.question: Through lot — Dad cut his arm a and it won't bleeding even when that.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now** if Dad's arm is still bleeding heavily or the bleeding won't stop. While you wait for help:

- **Press firmly** on the wound with a clean cloth, towel or bandage. Keep pressing without lifting to check.
- **If blood soaks through, add more cloth on top** rather than removing the first layer.
- **Raise the arm** above heart level if you can do it without hurting him.
- **Have him sit or lie down**, as heavy bleeding can make someone faint. Keep him warm.
- **Don't remove anything stuck in the wound**, and keep pressing the whole time.

Tell the 111 operator if Dad takes blood thinners (such as warfarin or apixaban), because these can make bleeding much harder to stop. If he's pale, dizzy, confused, drowsy or very weak, tell them that too. Keep in mind that someone with dementia may not be able to tell you how much pain or dizziness he's feeling, so go by what you can see.

This is frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once he's safe and the wound has been seen to, there's no need to cope alone. Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 for follow-up advice, and if the stress catches up with you, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor.

rows.question: husband is suddenly very agitated, stopped, shaking and says his heart reduce. He had chest pain let tie lock year.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Chest pain, shaking, and a past history of chest pain could mean a heart problem, and this needs emergency help straight away. Please don't wait to see if it passes.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Help him sit down and stay as still and calm as you can, in whatever position is most comfortable for him.
- Stay with him. Speak slowly and softly, and tell him help is coming.
- Loosen any tight clothing.
- Unlock the front door and turn on a light so paramedics can get in easily.
- Don't give him food, drink, or any medication unless the 111 operator tells you to. They can guide you over the phone.
- If you have his medication list and any diagnoses to hand, put them by the door for the paramedics.

If he becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the 111 operator straight away. They will talk you through what to do.

Sudden agitation, shaking, and fear can come from many things, including pain, a heart problem, or an infection. It is not something to put down to his dementia, and only a medical team can sort out the cause. You did exactly the right thing by reaching out, and I know this is frightening. You don't have to be certain what's wrong. Getting help early is always the right call.

Once he's with the paramedics and safe, please look after yourself too. If it all feels like too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: has vascular since myself, responding me skin is chair clammy.
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so please correct me if I've got this wrong. It sounds like you may be saying that someone has vascular dementia (a type of dementia caused by reduced blood flow to the brain), and that their skin feels clammy (cold, damp and sticky), perhaps while sitting in a chair.

If the clammy skin came on suddenly, or comes with any of the following, please call 111 straight away: chest pain or pressure, difficulty breathing, sudden facial droop, arm weakness or slurred speech, confusion that is worse than usual, or being very drowsy or hard to wake. Because vascular dementia is linked to strokes and heart disease, sudden clamminess alongside these signs can be serious, and it's always better to be checked than to wait.

If none of that is happening and the clamminess is mild or ongoing, it's still worth getting looked at. Clammy skin can have many causes, including low blood sugar, infection, blood pressure changes, pain, a warm room, or anxiety, and a person with dementia may not be able to tell you how they feel. I can't tell which it is from here. You can call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7) to talk it through with a nurse, or book a GP visit soon. Noting when it happens, whether they've eaten or had enough to drink, and any other changes will help them work it out.

If I've misunderstood, tell me a bit more: who has the vascular dementia, and what's been happening with the skin? And if you're the one caring for them and feeling worn down, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor. I'm here to help however I can.

rows.question: have thought about taking away of mum's pills manage just my. I can't anymore.
rows.answer:
It sounds like you've been carrying this on your own for a long time, and "I can't anymore" tells me how heavy it has become. Wanting to take over Mum's pills isn't a failure. It's very common, and often a sensible step, because forgetting doses or doubling up is one of the real risks in dementia care [S1].

If by "taking away" you mean you looking after her medication, a few things make it safer and lighter for you. Keep the medicines in a locked box or cabinet, and ask her pharmacy about blister packs, where each day's doses are sealed together so you can see at a glance if one was missed or taken twice [S1]. Supervise each dose rather than leaving it to her, and keep a current medication list (names, doses, prescriber) at home and in her bag in case of an emergency [S1]. Don't split or crush tablets without checking with the pharmacist first, as some are slow-release [S1]. If you're unsure about a missed or doubled dose, call the pharmacist or GP rather than guessing [S1].

How you do it matters too. Many people feel more in control when they keep some say, so you might explain why in simple terms, or let her take the pills from your hand herself [S3]. If she resists or gets upset, try again later when she's calmer.

If you mean stopping or removing some of her medications altogether, please don't do that on your own, as some medicines can cause problems if stopped suddenly. Do raise it with her GP or pharmacist, though. Medications should be reviewed regularly, and you can ask whether each one is still helping or could be reduced [S1][S4].

You also shouldn't be managing all this alone. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can connect you with local support, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7. If the "I can't anymore" feeling is bigger than the pills, please call or

rows.question: Some drive home times now wheel the bend. it normal for carers?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so please tell me if I've got this wrong. It sounds like you may be asking about the person you care for having trouble driving, perhaps getting confused or struggling at bends when driving home. Or you may mean that you, as a carer, find yourself getting distracted or struggling at the wheel on the drive home. I'll cover both.

**If it's the person you care for:** Trouble with bends, intersections or familiar routes is a common early sign that driving skills are changing in dementia. Family often notice it before the person does [S1]. A diagnosis doesn't mean driving must stop immediately. It's an ongoing decision, and the best next step is to raise your concerns with their GP, who can arrange a formal occupational therapy driving assessment, which is more objective than anyone's own judgement [S1]. If they keep driving, their car insurer needs to be told about the diagnosis, as cover could be affected. It's also worth starting to plan other ways of getting around early, such as family rosters, community transport or a taxi account, so it feels less like a sudden loss [S1]. In the meantime, please don't secretly disable the car. It tends to damage trust without solving the problem [S1].

**If it's you, as the carer:** Struggling on the drive home is not unusual, and it's worth taking seriously. Persistent exhaustion, poor sleep and a constant mental load are all common in carers and can really affect concentration [S5]. Chronic sleep deprivation is a health issue, not just tiredness, so getting some help with night-time care or regular respite matters for your safety as well as your wellbeing [S2]. It's a good idea to mention this to your own GP and tell them you're a carer. If you feel too tired to drive safely, please pull over, rest, or ask someone else to take over.

I'm so sorry, that sounds really heavy. I want to check I've understood you, as your message was a bit jumbled: is your dad saying he wants to die, and you're not sure how to help or what to say?

**If he's in danger right now, or has talked about a plan to hurt himself, please call 111 straight away.** Stay with him and keep him safe until help arrives.

If he's said it but is safe at the moment, take it seriously and stay calm. You don't need the perfect words. Try something like: "Dad, I'm really glad you told me. It sounds like you're hurting. I'm here, and I'm not going anywhere." Don't argue or tell him he doesn't mean it. Gently ask what's behind it. In dementia, "I want to die" can come from pain, fear, loneliness, feeling like a burden, low mood, or confusion, and each has a different answer. It's also fine to ask directly whether he's thinking of hurting himself. Asking doesn't plant the idea, and it tells him it's safe to talk to you.

Please also get his GP involved soon. Depression is common in dementia and can be treated, and pain or other medical issues can drive these feelings. Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) can advise on next steps, and Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can support you both. For the person he's speaking to, 1737 (call or text, any time) connects you with a trained counsellor. That includes you, because hearing this from your dad is painful, and you deserve support too.

Shouting after weeks of broken sleep doesn't make you a bad carer. It makes you a human being who is running on empty, and nearly every dementia carer has been exactly where you are.

Sleep deprivation wears down patience and mood for anyone, and night waking is one of the hardest parts of dementia care. You can't pour from an empty cup, so getting you some rest matters for both of you. A few things may help. Ask your mum's GP to check for treatable causes of night waking, like pain, a urinary tract infection (a bladder infection that can cause sudden confusion), or a medication side effect [S2]. Daytime activity and exercise can help her sleep better at night [S2]. If she wakes and wanders, gently checking whether she needs the toilet, food, or a drink, and making her room as calming as possible, can sometimes settle things [S2]. Most importantly, try to get another person involved, whether that's a family member, a friend, or a paid professional, so you can have even one full night's sleep [S2]. Alzheimers New Zealand can also talk through options like respite care (a short break where someone else cares for your mum).

I also want to check on you. You didn't finish your last sentence, and I'm not sure how you're feeling. If you're feeling overwhelmed, hopeless, or having any thoughts of harming yourself, please call 111 right away. If it is that, you're not alone. Night waking is very common in dementia, and it's one of the hardest things for carers because your own sleep suffers too.

A few things often help. Keep fixed bed and wake times every day, get him outside in natural daylight each morning, and encourage gentle activity during the day. Limit daytime naps to 15 to 30 minutes, make lunch the bigger meal, and avoid caffeine and lots of fluids in the evening [S2][S4]. A calming routine before bed, like dimmed lights and soothing music, can settle him [S2]. A nightlight in the hallway and a clock that clearly shows day or night can help if he wakes disoriented [S4]. If he wakes confused, stay calm, reassure him, and guide him gently back to bed rather than chatting or turning on bright lights [S4]. Sometimes pain, needing the toilet, or an infection is behind sudden changes in sleep, so it's worth asking the GP to check [S5].

You also matter in this. Ongoing sleep loss is a health issue for carers, and your GP can help with it too [S4]. If the nights have become a crisis, you can ask your GP about a referral to the older persons' mental health service, which can assess him at home and make a plan [S5]. You can also call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice) or the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001. I want to be honest with you: tying her into a chair isn't safe, and I can't help with ways to do it. Restraints (anything that stops someone moving freely, including ties, belts, or sheets) can cause serious harm. People struggle against them, and can strangle, fall while trying to climb out, injure their skin and circulation, or become more distressed and agitated. They're also not considered acceptable practice in dementia care.

The good news is there are safer ways to protect her.

**If she keeps getting up, ask what she's trying to do.** She may need the toilet, be in pain, be bored or restless, be thirsty, or be looking for something or someone. Meeting that need often settles the behaviour. A regular toileting routine, a drink, a gentle walk together, or something to do with her hands can make a big difference.

**Make the chair and space safer:**
- A supportive chair with arms, at the right height so she can stand safely, and a firm cushion rather than one she sinks into.
- Clear the floor of rugs and clutter, and keep lighting good, with a nightlight if it's evening or overnight [S3][S5].
- Well-fitting, flat, non-slip enclosed shoes rather than loose slippers or socks [S2][S5].
- Position the chair where you can see her, so you can guide her up safely when she wants to move.

**Get professional support.** Ask her GP for a medication review, as some medicines cause dizziness or drowsiness that raise fall risk, and for a referral to an occupational therapist for a home safety assessment [S5][S3]. A physio can assess her balance and strength. Alzheimers NZ can also help arrange assessments and talk through strategies on 0800 004 001. If she's eligible, a NASC (Needs Ass

I'm sorry, it sounds like you're exhausted and stretched very thin. I want to make sure I understand you: are you asking whether it's okay to lock your Dad in his room at night so you can sleep? Please correct me if I've misread you.

If so, I'd gently advise against locking him in. Even with the best intentions, it can be dangerous. If there's a fire, a fall, or he needs the toilet and can't get out, he may panic or be hurt and you wouldn't be able to reach him quickly. Being locked in can also increase fear and agitation, which often makes night-time confusion worse. And it can be unsafe or unlawful to confine someone without proper assessment and safeguards.

There are safer ways to get the rest you need. Door alarms and stair gates can alert you if he gets up, without restraining him [S1]. A nightlight between the bedroom and bathroom, and a clock that clearly shows day or night, can help him orient himself [S1]. Calm responses help too: guide him gently back to bed without bright lights or long conversations [S1]. Ask whether he needs the toilet, a drink, or something to eat, as meeting those needs may settle him [S2]. Daytime exercise, daylight, limiting naps, and a regular bedtime routine can all reduce night waking [S1][S3].

Please don't carry this alone. Ask a family member, friend, or paid carer to take a night or weekend so you can sleep [S2]. Long-term sleep loss is a health issue, not just tiredness, so tell your GP, both about Dad's sleep (they can check for causes like pain, infection, or medication effects) and about your own [S1][S5]. Alzheimers NZ suggests encouraging around 8-10 glasses (1500-2000 millilitres) of fluid a day, such as water, soup, juice, or iced lollies. Tea and coffee aren't counted toward that total [S1]. Tea is still fine to offer as a pleasant drink, it just shouldn't be the only source of fluid.

If your question was about something sudden, such as a sudden change in the person's behaviour, energy, or alertness, please tell me more. A sudden change can sometimes be a sign of dehydration, an infection, or another medical issue. If the person is hard to wake, has collapsed, or shows stroke signs like facial droop, arm weakness, or slurred speech, call 111 straight away. For anything less urgent, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7.

I can't give a dose for any sleep medicine, though. Sleep medicines can be risky for people with dementia, including increased confusion, drowsiness and a higher risk of falls, and the right choice depends on their other medicines and health. Please talk to their GP or pharmacist before giving anything, and don't start, stop or change a medicine without that advice.

Medicine is usually not the first step anyway. Good guidelines recommend a combination of non-drug approaches first: daytime exposure to natural light (a morning walk is ideal), gentle physical activity, personalised daytime activities, and consistent bed and wake times [S3][S5]. Limiting long daytime naps and evening caffeine can also help [S5]. If they wake at night, stay calm, keep lights low, and gently guide them back to bed rather than starting a long conversation. A nightlight between bedroom and bathroom and a clock that clearly shows day versus night can reduce fear and confusion [S5]. It also helps to check whether they need the toilet, a drink or a snack, or whether comfort like a blanket, soft music or a gentle massage would settle them [S2].

It's also worth asking the GP to check for a physical cause such as pain, a urinary tract infection (a bladder infection, which can cause confusion and restlessness), or a medicine side effect [S2][S3]. If the sleepiness or confusion came on suddenly rather than gradually, ask for same-day advice, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, with a registered nurse). If they can't be woken or seem unwell in a way that frightens you, call 111.

The quickest way to get a safe answer is to call your pharmacist or Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, with nurse advice). Have the packet or name of the medication ready and tell them what time he usually takes it and how late he is. If it's a supplement like turmeric, ask them about that too, as turmeric can interact with some medications, particularly blood thinners.

Missed doses happen to every caregiver, so please don't be hard on yourself. If it keeps happening, a pill organiser with days and times, a phone alarm, or asking the pharmacy about blister packs can help a lot. If he seems unwell, drowsy, or unusual in any way, call 111.

Your concern is a valid one. Antipsychotics carry real risks in older people with dementia, including a higher risk of stroke and falls [S1][S2], which is why they should only be used with careful oversight and reviewed regularly. If it's making them drowsy, unsteady, stiff, or "not themselves," that's exactly what the GP needs to hear, and asking "Is this still the right medicine?" is a perfectly reasonable question. Best practice is to look for the unmet need, discomfort, or trigger behind the behaviour first, and the GP can refer to a Mental Health Service for Older People for a specialist assessment and a person-centred plan [S1][S2].

If they seem very drowsy, hard to wake, have sudden facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech, or trouble breathing, call 111 straight away.

rows.answer:
It sounds like you're doing everything you can to make sure the tablets actually get taken. It's really common for people with dementia to spit tablets out or refuse them, and it's stressful to manage.

Please check with the pharmacist before crushing any more, though. Some tablets, especially slow-release or coated ones, can be harmful if the coating is broken, because the whole dose can hit the body at once. Others work less well, taste very bitter, or shouldn't be mixed with certain foods. Pharmacists advise against splitting, crushing, or dissolving tablets without their input [S2]. This isn't about doing anything wrong so far. It just depends on which medication it is. Some are fine to crush, and the pharmacist can tell you which.

The good news is that a pharmacist can usually help solve the underlying problem. Many medications come in liquid, dissolvable, or patch forms, and they can tell you whether there's an alternative. Don't change anything yourself, though. Switching forms or stopping a medication should always go through the GP or pharmacist. If tablets are being refused or spat out regularly, it's also worth telling the GP, since a medication review may help, and it's worth checking for swallowing difficulty if you notice coughing, choking, or food pooling in the cheek [S1][S2].

If you're unsure about something you've already given, or a dose was spat out and you don't know how much was swallowed, call the pharmacist or GP rather than guessing [S2]. Healthline (0800 611 116) is also free and has nurses available 24/7 if it's out of hours.

If it would help, tell me which type of medication it is in general terms (for example, "a heart tablet" or "a tablet for mood") and I can explain what to ask the pharmacist.

rows.question: that okay Dad have beers his donepezil medication?
rows.answer:
It's thoughtful of you to check, and the honest answer is that it depends on your dad, so it's best confirmed with his GP or pharmacist.

Donepezil (a medication that helps memory and thinking in Alzheimer's and Lewy body dementia) isn't known to have a dramatic, dangerous reaction with alcohol the way some medicines do. But alcohol can add to side effects such as dizziness, drowsiness and stomach upset, and nausea and appetite loss are already common with donepezil [S1]. Alcohol also tends to hit people with dementia harder. It can worsen confusion, memory, mood, sleep and balance, which raises the risk of falls, especially in the evening. If your dad takes other medicines such as sleeping tablets, anxiety medicines or antipsychotics, alcohol can combine with them in ways that are riskier [S2]. This is exactly the sort of thing to raise at his regular medication review [S3].

If his GP says a little is fine, a few things help. Keep it small, with food rather than on an empty stomach. Watch how he is afterwards, for more confusion, unsteadiness or sleepiness. Be aware that he may forget he's already had one, so it can help to pour for him rather than leave bottles within reach. Alcohol-free or low-alcohol beer can be a good way to keep the ritual and enjoyment without the risk.

You can ring his pharmacist or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7 nurse advice) for a quick answer, or the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) if you'd like to talk it through. And if he ever seems very drowsy, hard to wake, or suddenly much more confused or unsteady after drinking, call 111.

Meanwhile, here's what I can say. If you mean medicine for sleep, please don't buy anything over the counter without checking first. Some common sleep aids can worsen confusion and increase the risk of falls in people with dementia [S3]. A chemist is a good person to ask, because they can check anything new against the current medicines list, but I can't recommend a specific product or dose. Your GP or pharmacist is the right person for that.

If you mean non-medicine ways to help sleep, these often make a real difference: keep consistent bed and wake times every day, get morning daylight and gentle activity, avoid long daytime naps and evening caffeine or alcohol, and use a nightlight on the way to the bathroom [S1]. A clock that clearly shows day or night beside the bed can also help if they wake confused [S1].

If the issue is the opposite, that they've become **suddenly very sleepy or drowsy**, that needs same-day advice. Call your GP, or Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7). Call 111 straight away if they can't be woken, aren't responding normally, or have new weakness, a drooping face or trouble speaking [S5].

If lack of sleep is wearing you down too, please mention it to your GP, as carer exhaustion matters. You can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor. Tell me a bit more about what's happening and I'll help from there.

rows.question: My mother-in-law takes 8 different tablets. own can safely drop much?
rows.answer:
Eight tablets is a lot to keep track of, and it's a good instinct to question whether every one is still needed. The key point is that no one outside her prescriber team can safely say which tablets can be dropped, and I can't either. Some medicines are dangerous to stop suddenly (heart, blood pressure and seizure medicines, for example), while others may genuinely be worth reducing. Please don't stop or skip any yourselves, even ones that seem unimportant.

What you can do is ask for a full medication review with her GP or pharmacist. Medicines that suited her at diagnosis can become unsuitable as dementia progresses, so reviewing the whole list at least every six months is recommended [S1]. It helps to bring every tablet she takes, including over-the-counter products and supplements, plus a current list showing each drug's name, dose, frequency and prescriber [S1]. At the review, ask of each medicine: What is this for? Is it still doing that job? What are the side effects, and could any be adding to confusion, drowsiness or falls? Could it be reduced or stopped safely, and how would that be monitored? That last question matters most for sedating or psychotropic medicines (those that act on mood, behaviour or sleep). These carry real risks in dementia, and the aim is to review them regularly and reduce or stop them where they're no longer helping, ideally after non-drug approaches to distress have been tried [S3][S5]. Any change should be planned and supervised by the prescriber.

In the meantime, keep her tablets locked away and use a pharmacy blister pack, so a missed or doubled dose is easy to spot [S1]. Supervise each dose rather than relying on reminders alone. If you're unsure about a missed or doubled dose, call her pharmacist or GP rather than guessing [S1]. Never crush, split or dissolve tablets without pharm

One general point in case it's useful. At her age and weight, bone strength and fall risk are worth raising with her GP, who can assess her properly and refer her to an occupational therapist or physiotherapist. They can also advise on safe transfers and equipment. If you're lifting or supporting her yourself, please look after your own back too. Guide her movement rather than taking her full weight, and never try to catch her if she falls. Guide her down gently and call for help instead.

rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're seeing this with your dad. It can be very unsettling for you both, and wanting a straight answer is completely understandable. I'm not completely sure I've read your message right, so please correct me: I think you're asking whether Dad seeing animals that aren't there, and perhaps a shadow or something moving as he walks, could be dementia.

Seeing things that aren't there (hallucinations) can happen in some types of dementia, especially Lewy body dementia (a type that often affects movement, alertness and vivid visual hallucinations, commonly of people or animals), and sometimes in the middle or later stages of other types [S2]. But I can't tell you whether this is dementia. Hallucinations can also come from other causes, and only a proper assessment from his GP can sort out which it is.

The most important thing: if these experiences started suddenly, it could be delirium (a sudden state of confusion, often triggered by infection, pain, dehydration, constipation or a medication change), and that needs to be seen by a doctor promptly [S2]. If Dad is very drowsy, hard to wake, or suddenly much worse, please call 111. Otherwise, a GP visit soon is a good idea either way. Poor eyesight or hearing can also cause people to misread what they see, so those are worth checking too [S2].

In the meantime, a few things help:
- **Stay calm and reassure him.** What he sees feels completely real to him. Try something like "You're safe, I'm here with you." Arguing that the animals aren't there tends to increase his fear [S2].
- **Check the environment.** Shadows, patterned rugs, reflections, and dim corners can look like animals. Brighter lighting and a good night light can make a big difference [S2].

rows.question: husband 54 forgetting. early-onset dementia? need know before we tell kids.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry you're facing this worry. Noticing changes in your husband and carrying the question of what to tell your children is a heavy load, and it makes sense to want answers first.

I can't tell you whether this is early-onset dementia (dementia diagnosed before 65), and only a proper assessment can. At 54, memory changes can have many causes, including stress, depression, poor sleep, thyroid or vitamin problems, medication effects, and other treatable conditions, so it's worth not assuming the worst. The next step is a GP visit. It helps to bring a written list of examples with dates, and if he's willing, go together. Dementia in younger people often shows up differently, with changes in behaviour, personality, or language rather than memory loss first, and these are easily mistaken for stress or low mood [S1]. So mention any changes like that too, even if they seem unrelated. If he is diagnosed, people under 65 can be assessed for funded support through their local NASC (the local needs assessment service) [S1].

You don't have to wait for a diagnosis to get support. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk through what you're seeing, and the Younger Onset Dementia Aotearoa Trust (yodat.org.nz) supports families in exactly your situation [S1]. If the waiting and worry are weighing on you, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

On the kids, you don't need to have a diagnosis before you say something. Children often sense that something is wrong and fill the gaps with their own fears. Until you know more, you can keep it simple and honest, for example: "Dad has been having some memory trouble, and we're going to the doctor to find out why." If dementia is confirmed, simple, concrete explanations work best, along with repeatedly reassuring them that no one caused it and it isn't contagious [S2

rows.question: year give mum the memory test I cold do morning home to confirm has dementia?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you've noticed changes in Mum and want some answers, which can feel scary and urgent. That's a very understandable place to be.

Unfortunately, there isn't a test you can safely give at home to confirm dementia, and I'd gently encourage you not to try. A home test can't tell you the cause. Memory problems can come from things that are treatable and reversible, like some medications, thyroid problems, low vitamin B12, anaemia, infections, depression, or poor sleep. A proper assessment looks for these [S5]. Testing Mum yourself could also cause her real distress, especially if she senses she's being "tested" and struggles. That can damage trust at a time when you want her to feel safe with you.

The best next step is a GP visit. Your GP will take a detailed history, review her medications, do cognitive screening tests (short, standardised memory and thinking checks), and order blood tests to rule out treatable causes. If needed, they can refer her to a specialist for further assessment [S5]. Before the appointment, it helps to jot down specific examples you've noticed: what changed, when, and how it affects daily life. Things to watch for include forgetting recent events, trouble with familiar tasks, confusion about time or place, difficulty finding words, withdrawal from hobbies, or mood and personality changes [S1]. It can help to tell the GP beforehand, privately or in writing, so the appointment goes smoothly. If Mum is reluctant, you could frame it as a general health check.

For guidance on how to raise this with Mum, you can call the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001 or contact your local Dementia NZ service [S1]. If you're feeling worried or overwhelmed, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. rows.question: I'm going away the nights. moderate is fine house on your drive. Can I leave her?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so please correct me if I've got it wrong. It sounds like you're asking whether you can leave your loved one with dementia alone overnight while you're away, perhaps because she seems to be managing "moderately" well at home. Is that right?

If so, I'd gently say that for most people with dementia at a moderate stage, being alone overnight isn't safe, even if she copes well during the day. Evenings and nights are often when confusion worsens (sometimes called "sundowning", where restlessness and disorientation increase later in the day). She may get up disoriented, try to leave the house, fall, or be unable to manage the stove, heating, or a medical problem. Wandering is a real risk at night, so a secure home, door alarms, and a safe outdoor space matter, but they don't replace having a person there [S4]. If she did leave, nobody would know. If she's been needing reassurance when she feels lost or wants to "go home", she'll need someone who can give it [S1].

Here are some options for the nights you're away:
- Ask a trusted family member or friend to stay with her, ideally someone she knows well, in her own home so her surroundings stay familiar.
- Arrange respite care (planned short-term care so you can have a break). Your local Dementia NZ or Alzheimers NZ service can help you explore this, and a NASC (Needs Assessment and Service Coordination) assessment can unlock funded respite options. Call Alzheimers NZ on 0800 004 001.
- Look at a short respite stay in a care facility with dementia-trained staff, if home cover isn't possible.

If you're unsure how much she can safely manage, her GP or Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) can help you think it through.

Taking a break is a good thing, and carers who rest are better able to keep going. Could you tell me

rows.question: She keeps leaving the hob on. A was thinking of just turning gas i off at the mains permanently letting her used the melatonin. Sensible? Bye.
rows.answer:
It's really worrying when the hob keeps getting left on, and wanting to act on it makes complete sense. Repeated incidents like this are a signal that more safety measures are needed, even if nothing has gone wrong yet [S5].

Turning the gas off at the mains is a legitimate option. Taking away the hazard is often the most reliable fix, as the passages suggest removing stove knobs or disabling appliances when unsupervised use isn't safe [S5]. The main downside is that she loses her ability to make herself a hot meal or drink, so you'd want a plan for that. Some gentler middle steps could work too: a stove guard or automatic shut-off device, or an induction cooktop that only heats when a pan is present [S5]. A heat-activated kitchen alarm and interconnected smoke alarms add a safety net, and Fire and Emergency NZ (fireandemergency.nz) may offer a free home safety visit [S4]. If you can, keep her involved in the kitchen with simple tasks alongside you, so she keeps a sense of purpose [S5].

On the melatonin, I'm not sure I've followed what you mean. If you're thinking of her using it for sleep, that's a decision for her GP or pharmacist, and I can't advise on starting it or on dosing. It also wouldn't solve the hob problem, so please don't let it be the thing you rely on. If sleep is part of the picture, a GP check is worthwhile, as poor sleep can have medical causes such as infection, pain or medication effects [S1]. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also give free nurse advice any time.

Whatever you choose, make sure you have a way to check in on how she's coping day to day. If this is all landing on you, it's a lot to carry. The Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can talk through practical options, and you can call

rows.question: The that okay let Dad have a hot bath on I check 20 minutes?
rows.answer:
Your question came through a bit garbled, so please correct me if I've misread it. I think you're asking whether it's okay to let Dad have a hot bath on his own and just check on him every 20 minutes.

I'd gently say no, that isn't a safe arrangement. With dementia, a person may not recognise water that's too hot, or may not react to it, and at 60°C serious burns can happen within seconds [S3]. A lot can go wrong in 20 minutes: a slip or fall (the bathroom is the highest-risk room in the home for falls), scalding, or becoming confused or unable to get out of the bath [S5]. Falls in people with dementia are especially dangerous because injuries may not be noticed or reported straight away [S5]. If you ever find Dad has fallen, can't be woken, or seems injured in the bath, call 111 straight away.

There are some practical things that can make bathing safer and calmer. Set the hot water thermostat to a maximum of 50°C, which is a one-off fix that protects him even when you're not right there [S3]. A bath seat or shower chair and a handheld showerhead make washing safer, as do grab rails and non-slip mats [S5][S4]. Warm the bathroom and have towels and clothes ready beforehand, and keep a towel over his shoulders to preserve his dignity and keep him warm [S4][S1]. If he's anxious, a calm "I'm not going to let you get hurt" can ease resistance [S4], and if he refuses, it's fine to try again later or on another day [S4].

If he values his privacy, you can stay within reach without hovering over him: keep him covered, let him do what he can himself, and give him some quiet space while you stay close enough to hear or step in. It's also worth asking whether he'd prefer a shower, or whether someone else, perhaps a support worker, might be more comfort

rows.question: friend said turmeric capsules to decisions. How many should Mum take the dad?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure what your friend suggested. Your message seems to have a few words missing, so please correct me if I've misread it. I'm guessing it's about turmeric capsules for your mum, who has dementia, and possibly for helping with her thinking or decision-making.

I can't give you a number of capsules. Doses for supplements and medicines are a decision for your mum's GP or pharmacist, and it matters more than it might seem. Turmeric (curcumin, the active ingredient) can interact with common medicines, especially blood thinners like warfarin or aspirin, and with some diabetes and stomach medicines. It can also affect the liver in some people. Research hasn't shown that turmeric reliably improves memory or thinking in people with dementia, so I wouldn't want you to count on it, even though your friend means well.

Before giving any supplement, I'd suggest taking the bottle to your mum's pharmacist or GP and asking if it's safe alongside her current medicines. Keeping an up-to-date list of everything she takes, supplements included, helps with this [S3]. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also give free nurse advice any time if you'd like a quick answer.

If you're hoping to support your mum with decisions, there are practical approaches that can really help. Offering just two or three simple choices, and asking at the time of day when she's calmest, can make everyday decisions much easier for her [S1]. For bigger decisions, explaining things plainly and in her own terms helps her stay involved [S1]. If it would help, I'm happy to go through ideas for this, or if I've misunderstood what you were asking, tell me a bit more and I'll do my best.

rows.question: I read aluminium his Assessment. this cookware?
rows.answer:
Your message came through a bit garbled, so I'm not completely sure what you're asking. It sounds like you may be asking whether aluminium cookware causes or worsens dementia. If so, here's the short answer. Concern about aluminium has been around for decades, but large studies have not found convincing evidence that cooking in aluminium pots and pans causes Alzheimer's disease or other dementias. Everyday exposure from cookware is small, and the research on this is not entirely settled, but major dementia organisations don't advise people to throw their cookware out for this reason. If it gives you peace of mind, stainless steel or glass are easy alternatives, but there's no need to worry that you've caused harm.

The more important cookware question is often about safety rather than the material. For someone with dementia, the bigger risks are pans left on a hot stove, burns, or boiling dry. Practical steps include an automatic stove shut-off device, switching to an induction cooktop that only heats when a pan is present, and watching for patterns such as forgotten food or near-misses over recent weeks, which suggest more safeguards are needed [S1]. An occupational therapist (a health professional who assesses how someone manages daily tasks and their home) can do a full home safety assessment. You can arrange one through your GP or a needs assessment, or ask Alzheimers NZ for help on 0800 004 001 [S2].

If you meant something different, such as a home safety assessment, a specific person's cooking safety, or something else you read, just let me know and I'll gladly help. And if caring for someone is weighing on you, you can always call or text 1737 to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: The flu jab neighbour's homecare drinking. It's letting Dad have you, rather?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, but I'm having trouble making sense of your message. It looks like some words may have got jumbled or cut off, possibly from voice-to-text or typing on a phone. I don't want to guess and give you advice that misses what you actually need.

Could you tell me again, in your own words, what's happening with your Dad? It sounds like it might involve a few things:

- **The flu jab**: whether Dad should have one, or whether he's had a reaction
- **Your neighbour helping out**: perhaps with homecare or looking in on him
- **Drinking**: either Dad not drinking enough fluids, or alcohol

If you're thinking about fluids, it's very common for people with dementia to lose the sense of thirst, so they can become dehydrated without realising. A gentle routine of offering drinks through the day, and keeping a simple record of what he has, can help [S2].

Please take your time. If Dad seems unwell right now, such as very drowsy, confused more than usual, or hard to wake, call 111 straight away. If you just want to talk something through with a nurse, Healthline is free on 0800 611 116, 24/7.

And if you're feeling stretched thin, that's completely understandable. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can also help you find local support.

What's on your mind with Dad?

rows.question: clinic i'm Thailand shops stem-cell cure vascular dementia. It costs $40,000. it week i'm?
rows.answer:
I'm not sure I've understood your message fully, so please tell me if I've got this wrong. It sounds like a clinic in Thailand is offering stem-cell treatment for vascular dementia (dementia caused by reduced blood flow to the brain) at around $40,000, and you're deciding whether to go.

I'd urge real caution before paying. At present there is no stem-cell treatment proven to cure or reverse any type of dementia. Brain cells and blood vessels damaged by strokes can't currently be repaired this way, and what's sold by private clinics is largely unproven. These treatments can carry risks such as infection, and some can be harmful. Anyone promising a "cure" for a condition like this should be treated with scepticism, and a high price doesn't indicate it works. If this is for someone you care for, the travel itself can also be hard on a person with dementia, since unfamiliar places often increase confusion and distress.

Before committing any money, please talk to their GP or specialist about what the clinic is offering. You can also call Alzheimers NZ on 0800 004 001, or Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7), to talk it through. They hear about these offers often, and no one will judge you for asking.

What can make a real difference with vascular dementia is managing the underlying causes: blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, and staying active. Because vascular dementia can progress in steps after further small strokes, keeping on top of these is one of the most direct ways to reduce the risk of further decline [S5]. Structured routines and breaking tasks into clear steps also help people hold on to daily function [S5]. If you want to explore other options, there are also programmes like Cognitive Stimulation Therapy (a group programme of themed activities and conversation) that may help in the mild-to-moderate stages, and your GP can tell you what

rows.question: Since just ageing, point seeing the doctor about Mum's?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you've noticed something in Mum that's worried you, and you're wondering whether it's worth a doctor's visit or just part of getting older. That uncertainty is really common, and it's worth acting on.

Dementia (a group of conditions that affect memory, thinking and daily functioning) is not a normal part of ageing [S1]. Occasional forgetfulness, like losing a name or misplacing keys but remembering later, is within the normal range. What's different is when changes are more persistent, getting worse over time, and starting to get in the way of daily life [S1]. Signs that suggest it's time to book a GP visit include:

- Forgetting recent events, names or faces, or repeating questions
- Struggling with familiar tasks, like a known recipe, managing money, or a familiar driving route
- Confusion about time or place, or trouble finding words
- Misplacing things and being unable to retrace steps
- Withdrawing from hobbies or friends
- Mood or personality changes, such as new anxiety, suspicion or irritability [S1]

Seeing the GP is worthwhile even if it turns out not to be dementia. Memory and thinking changes can also come from treatable things like depression, infections, medication side effects, low vitamin levels or an underactive thyroid [S4]. The GP can work out which it is through a medical history, a physical check, blood tests, memory testing and sometimes brain imaging [S4]. If it is dementia, earlier diagnosis means earlier support and gives Mum time to have a say in planning her own care [S1].

It helps to jot down specific examples, when each thing first happened and whether it's getting worse, and bring that note to the appointment [S4]. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk through what you're seeing and what support is available.

rows.question: My mum dementia fell down the stairs and she is need responding walk I to her. he What should To do?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** A fall down the stairs with your mum not responding could mean a serious head, neck or spine injury, so she needs an ambulance straight away.

While you wait for help:
- **Don't move her**, unless she is in immediate danger. Moving her could make a neck or back injury worse.
- **Stay with her** and talk to her calmly, even if she isn't answering. Tell her help is on its way.
- **Check she is breathing.** The 111 operator can talk you through what to do if she isn't, or if she is bleeding.
- **If she is bleeding,** press gently on the wound with a clean cloth.
- **Keep her warm** with a blanket or coat over her, without moving her body.
- **Unlock the front door** or send someone to meet the ambulance, and have her medication list ready for the paramedics.

I know how frightening this is. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once the ambulance arrives, the paramedics will take over and look after both of you.

Even if she wakes up and seems okay, she still needs to be checked. After any fall, people with dementia can have fractures or head injuries without being able to tell you they're in pain [S2].

Afterwards, once she is safe, we can talk about making the stairs safer, like non-slip treads, secure banisters, and nightlights, and about an occupational therapy home assessment. For now, please make that 111 call. If you feel overwhelmed afterwards, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Dad's face suddenly looks droopy on one and his speech is slurred. Should I just is keep an eye on to overnight?
rows.answer:
**Please call 111 right now. Don't wait overnight.**

A sudden droopy face and slurred speech are warning signs of a stroke (a blockage or bleed in the brain). Stroke treatment works best when it starts within the first hours, so waiting to "see how he is in the morning" could cost him a lot. Even if the signs seem to come and go, he still needs to be seen urgently [S3].

While you wait for the ambulance, note the time you first noticed the changes, as the paramedics and hospital will ask. Keep him sitting or lying comfortably and stay with him. Don't give him food, drink or tablets, as swallowing may be affected. If you can, have his medication list and any diagnoses (including dementia) ready to hand to the ambulance crew, and unlock the door for them.

I know how frightening this is, and you're doing the right thing by checking. It's always better to call and have it turn out to be nothing than to wait. If you feel overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. For now, please make that 111 call.

rows.question: My husband with dementia is clutching his some it in prevent. What do I do?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're in this situation. Your message got a bit jumbled, so I want to check I'm understanding: are you saying your husband is clutching something and won't let go, or clutching a part of his body, such as his stomach or groin area, as though he's in discomfort?

**If he's clutching his chest, he's having trouble breathing, or he seems to be in sudden severe pain, call 111 now.** The same goes if he has swallowed something harmful (for example, if he's clutching or has put a household product, soap, or tablets in his mouth).

If he is holding his stomach, lower belly, or groin, it could be pain or a need to use the toilet that he can't express. In dementia, a urinary tract infection (UTI), constipation, or simply needing the toilet are common and easily missed causes of this kind of behaviour [S2]. A UTI can also cause sudden confusion or worsening of dementia symptoms, so it warrants prompt medical attention. Try gently offering the toilet and a drink, and watch for other signs such as grimacing, restlessness, or a change in his urine. If you suspect pain or infection, call his GP, or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice).

If he's holding onto an object, like a bag, cloth, or something from the house, that is often a way of seeking comfort or security. Try not to pull it away. Instead, sit beside him, speak calmly, and ask about it, or offer a swap for something safe he can hold. If it could be harmful (such as a tablet, chemical, or sharp item), gently trade it for something he likes rather than taking it by force, as being startled can lead to distress or lashing out [S1]. Keeping medications and household chemicals locked away helps prevent this situation in future [S3][S4].
