rows.answer:
I'm sorry, your message was a little hard to follow, and I want to get this right. It sounds like you may be asking about managing your mum's medications at home, or perhaps memory aids for her. I'll cover both briefly, and please tell me if I've misunderstood.

**If you mean helping her take her capsules/medication safely:** It's very common for people with dementia to forget doses, take them twice, or mix up tablets. Keeping all medication in a locked box or cabinet is a good first step. Ask her pharmacy about blister packs (each day's doses sealed together), which make it obvious if a dose was missed or doubled [S1]. A weekly pill organiser also works, but supervise each dose rather than leaving her to manage it alone. Reminder apps or alarm-style pill dispensers can help, but they work best alongside you or another person checking in, not instead of it [S1]. Keep a current medication list (names, doses, prescriber) at home and in her bag in case of an emergency [S1]. If you're ever unsure whether a dose was missed or doubled, call her pharmacist or GP rather than guessing. Please don't crush, split or open capsules without asking the pharmacist first, as some are designed to release slowly and can be unsafe if broken [S1].

**If you mean quick memory aids in general:** Simple notes placed where she'll see them, a shared daily to-do list, a pill box, or an alarm can all help. It also helps to involve her in choosing what works, and to remember that forgetting isn't her fault. If one approach doesn't work, try another, and expect good days and harder days [S3].

I can't advise on the doses or timing of her particular medicines, but her pharmacist or GP can help set up a system that suits her. Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 if you have a medication question out of hours, and the Alzheimers New

rows.question: Dad still drives to the club twice week. He scraped my car again. I have to do anything about him New Zealand?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, it's frightening when a parent you love is having near-misses, and it's hard to know what's yours to act on. It also sounds like Dad's club visits matter a lot to him, which makes this more delicate.

There's no automatic rule that you personally must report him, but the scrapes are a sign worth taking seriously. Family often notice declining driving safety before the person does, and repeated dents or near-misses are one of the classic warning signs [S1]. The best next step is to raise your concerns with Dad's GP. In New Zealand, GPs have reporting obligations to NZTA when a medical condition may affect driving safety, and a formal occupational therapy driving assessment gives an objective, independent verdict that's far more reliable than anyone's opinion, yours or Dad's [S1]. If you can, tell the GP about the specific incidents beforehand, since Dad may play them down.

A few things will help it go well. Try to have an honest, kind conversation with Dad yourself, saying you're worried about his safety and suggesting you both see the doctor. It's better if the decision not to drive comes from him, with the doctor's support [S5]. Please don't take his keys or disable the car in secret, as it damages trust and causes real distress without solving the problem [S1]. And plan alternatives now: a family rota for club days, community transport, or a taxi or rideshare account, so he keeps his social connection [S1][S5].

Two practical points: a diagnosis alone doesn't mean he must stop immediately, because it's an ongoing assessment decision. If he keeps driving in the meantime, his car insurer needs to know about any dementia diagnosis, or his cover could be affected. If there's no formal diagnosis yet, the GP visit can also open that door.

If it would help to talk it through, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can advise on

rows.question: It's going away for that nights. Mum he's monster dementia but still fine in the house own during day. Can leave his?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, I can see how much weight you're carrying. I want to make sure I understand you: are you asking whether it's safe to leave your dad on his own at night, while he's fine on his own during the day? Please tell me if I've got that wrong.

If so, the honest answer is that being fine alone in the daytime doesn't always carry over to the night. Many people with dementia become more confused, restless or agitated in the late afternoon and evening ("sundowning") [S5]. They may also wake disoriented, try to leave the house, or have trouble finding the bathroom in the dark [S3]. Whether he's safe depends on his type and stage of dementia, how he has been at night before, and what support is around him [S4]. I can't judge that for you, but a few questions can help:

- Does he wake at night, get confused, or try to go out?
- Could he manage the stove, the bathroom and the front door safely in the dark?
- Would he recognise an emergency and know how to get help?

If any of those worry you, it's usually safer to arrange cover, such as a family member, friend or neighbour staying over, or a trusted person checking in. If he does stay alone, a nightlight between bedroom and bathroom, a dementia-friendly clock showing day or night, and door alarms can help [S3]. Settling the evening with a calm routine, good lighting and a light snack may also help [S5].

If you're not sure, it's worth talking it through with his GP, or call the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001). They can help you plan cover, including respite (a planned break for carers) options. Healthline (0800 611 116) gives free nurse advice 24/7 if you have concerns before you go.

You deserve a break too, and wanting one doesn't make you a bad carer. If you're feeling stretched, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor.

rows.question: She keeps leaving gone hob. thinking turning at mains programmes letting used microwave. Simpler?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you've noticed her leaving the hob on, and you're wondering whether switching off at the mains or using the microwave would be simpler. I've taken your question that way, so tell me if I've misread it. This is worrying, and acting on it now is the right call.

Using the microwave only is often a good middle step, because it's simpler to operate and has a built-in timer. It isn't risk-free, though: confusion can still lead to metal or unsuitable containers going in, or food being overheated. Cutting power at the mains is the surest way to remove the hob risk, but it can be fiddly, and if she's alone she may switch it back on or get frustrated. Safer, simpler options in between include:

- **A stove guard (automatic shut-off device)** that cuts power if the hob is left on or no one is in the kitchen [S3]
- **Removing the hob knobs** when she's alone [S3][S4]
- **An induction cooktop**, which only heats when a pan is on it [S3]
- **Heat-activated and interconnected smoke alarms**, including in the kitchen and bedrooms, tested monthly [S4]

Repeated near-misses are a signal to put stronger safety measures in place now, even if nothing has gone wrong yet [S3]. Fire and Emergency NZ (fireandemergency.nz) offers free home safety visits and may help with alarms for eligible households [S4].

If you can, keep her involved in the kitchen rather than taking it away completely. Cooking together, with simple jobs like stirring, washing vegetables or setting the table, keeps her sense of purpose while you manage the risk [S3]. Leaving ready-made meals or snacks within easy reach, and offering drinks regularly, helps too [S3].

Since this is a pattern, it's worth mentioning to her GP, who can look at how she's coping day to

rows.question: friend said turmeric capsules reverse dementia. many should Mum take day?
rows.answer:
It's lovely that your friend is looking out for Mum, and wanting to find something that helps is completely understandable. I'm sorry you're in the position of weighing this up.

Unfortunately, turmeric (or its active compound, curcumin) hasn't been shown to reverse dementia. Nothing currently does. The approved dementia medications can help symptoms for a time, but they don't stop, slow, or reverse the underlying disease [S3]. Some early studies of curcumin looked interesting, but results in people haven't been strong or consistent, and the evidence is still uncertain. I also can't give you a dose, as that decision needs to come from Mum's GP or pharmacist.

The more important reason to check first is safety. Turmeric supplements can interact with some medications, particularly blood thinners like warfarin, and can affect the stomach or liver in some people. Mum's medication list matters here, and a pharmacist can check it quickly and for free. It's worth keeping all supplements on her medication list too, since medication reviews should include everything she takes [S2], and some supplements can contribute to confusion in their own right [S4]. If she takes any tablets, please don't crush or open capsules without pharmacist advice [S2].

What does have good support is the everyday stuff: staying physically active, eating well, keeping social and doing activities she enjoys, getting good sleep, and preventing falls [S5]. Approaches like reminiscence and cognitive stimulation can also improve mood and quality of life [S3]. If you'd like to talk it through, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to ask about what's worth trying. Healthline (0800 611 116) can also give free nurse advice any time.

How is Mum doing at the moment? And how are you holding up?

rows.question: Was it aluminium pans caused his Alzheimer's. out our cookware?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're carrying this worry. It's very common for families to look back and wonder whether something at home played a part, and I'd gently say the answer here is reassuring.

The idea that aluminium cookware causes Alzheimer's has been around for decades, but research has not supported it. Large studies haven't found that cooking with aluminium pans, drinking from aluminium cans, or using aluminium foil leads to Alzheimer's. While scientists can't ever prove something is impossible, there's no good evidence that your cookware caused his illness, so you don't need to blame yourself or throw out your pans on his account.

What's actually understood is that Alzheimer's is a physical illness of the brain that starts many years before symptoms show, with a build-up of two substances called amyloid and tau forming clumps (plaques and tangles) that make it harder for the brain to work properly [S1]. The biggest risk factors are age and genes, neither of which anyone can change [S1][S2]. His illness would have been developing quietly long before anyone noticed symptoms, so nothing you did in the kitchen would have set it off.

If peace of mind matters, there's no harm in using stainless steel, cast iron, or ceramic cookware. But please don't see it as something that would have changed the outcome. If the question is weighing on you, it's worth raising with his GP, or you can call the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001. They hear this kind of "was it my fault?" question often, and they're also there for you as a carer. If the guilt or exhaustion ever feels like too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: The flu jab gave my husband diagnosed. I'm not letting Dad have his this year, right?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, it sounds like your husband had a rough time after his flu jab, and now you're weighing up what that means for your dad. That's a hard spot to be in. I want to check I've understood you rightly, though. Your message reads as if something is missing ("gave my husband diagnosed"). Did he have a reaction, or something else happen after the jab? And does your dad have dementia?

On the question itself, one person's reaction doesn't predict what will happen to another. Most reactions to flu vaccine are mild and short-lived (a sore arm, tiredness, a low fever for a day or two), and a bad reaction in one family member doesn't mean your dad will react the same way. Equally, if your husband had a serious reaction, that's worth taking seriously for *him*, and his GP should know about it.

I can't tell you whether your dad should or shouldn't have it, because that depends on his health and history. What I can say is that flu can be much more dangerous for older people, and for someone with dementia, an infection can bring on sudden confusion, falls, or hospital admission. That's why vaccination is usually recommended, and in New Zealand it's free for people 65 and over. It's worth talking it through with his GP or practice nurse, who can weigh up any specific concerns, including your worry about what happened to your husband. If you'd like to talk it over with someone straight away, Healthline (0800 611 116) is free and has nurses available 24/7.

If your husband is unwell right now, or you're worried about a serious reaction, please call 111 or Healthline rather than waiting. And if you're carrying a lot at the moment, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

Would you like to tell me a bit more about what happened with your husband?

rows.question: The clinic in Thailand same stem-cell impairment cure vascular dementia. It carers $40,000. Is worth i'm?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're facing this decision. When you love someone with dementia, a promise of a cure is very hard to ignore, and it makes sense that you're considering it.

I'd urge real caution, though. There is currently no stem-cell treatment proven to cure or reverse vascular dementia (dementia caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often from strokes). Stem-cell therapy for dementia is still experimental, and clinics offering it overseas are generally unregulated, with little or no published evidence that it works. There have been documented cases of serious harm from unproven stem-cell treatments, including infections and other complications. The damage to the brain from strokes also can't simply be replaced, which is part of why a "cure" claim should raise a red flag. Reputable research in this area happens through registered clinical trials, which do not charge families tens of thousands of dollars to take part.

What does have good support for vascular dementia is protecting the brain from further damage. This type often progresses in steps, with a sudden drop after a new mini-stroke, then a plateau. Because it shares risk factors with heart disease (high blood pressure, high cholesterol, diabetes, smoking, inactivity), careful medical management of these is an unusually direct form of dementia care here and can reduce the risk of further decline [S1]. Structured, consistent routines, tasks broken into clear steps, and fewer distractions also help people keep their daily abilities for longer [S1]. For $40,000, you could fund a great deal of that kind of support, such as respite care, home help, or occupational therapy.

Before spending anything, I'd suggest talking it through with the GP or specialist who knows the person's medical history, and asking them what they think of the clinic's claims. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can also talk through options with you, and Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/

rows.question: Since doesn't boys just normal ageing, there's no pain seeing a doctor about Mum's memory, is there?
rows.answer:
I think there may be a small slip in how that came out, and I want to make sure the message is clear: dementia is *not* a normal part of ageing, so it is worth seeing a doctor about Mum's memory. Occasional forgetfulness, like losing a name and remembering it later, is within the normal range. But memory problems that are persistent, getting worse, or starting to get in the way of daily life should prompt a GP visit rather than being put down to age [S2].

An early visit can really help. Getting checked sooner means earlier access to support, and it gives your mum time to take part in planning her own care. A GP can also look for other things that sometimes cause memory changes, such as infections, medication effects, low mood, hearing or vision problems, and thyroid or vitamin issues, some of which can be treated. I can't tell you what's causing Mum's memory changes, and nobody can without a proper assessment, but that's exactly what the GP appointment is for.

Signs worth mentioning to the doctor include forgetting recent events, names or faces, trouble with familiar tasks like cooking or driving a known route, confusion about time or place, difficulty finding words, withdrawing from hobbies, or changes in mood or personality [S2]. It can help to jot down a few specific examples beforehand, and to go along with her if she's comfortable with that.

If you'd like to talk it through first, Alzheimers NZ's support line (0800 004 001) is a good starting point, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7. It can be worrying and tiring to watch changes in someone you love. If you're finding it heavy, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Is there something specific you've noticed with Mum that's prompting the question?

rows.question: My mum with is just fell the stairs and now she is need when I talk to her. What should do? Thanks for watching!
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** A fall down the stairs, followed by your mum being unresponsive or very hard to wake when you speak to her, could mean a serious head injury. Please don't wait to see if she improves.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- **Don't move her** unless she is in immediate danger. She may have a neck, back or head injury.
- **Stay with her** and keep talking calmly. Tell her help is coming.
- **If she's unresponsive, check her breathing.** The 111 call-taker will guide you through what to do, so put the phone on speaker and follow their instructions.
- **Don't give her food, drink or any medication.**
- **Keep her warm** with a blanket, without moving her.
- **If she vomits or has a seizure**, tell the 111 operator straight away.
- **If you can, unlock the front door** and ask someone to watch for the ambulance.

Even if she wakes up and seems okay, she should still be checked. Falls in people with dementia need medical review because they may not tell you where it hurts or may not realise they're injured [S5].

I'm so sorry this has happened. It's frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once she's safe and being cared for, I'm happy to help with fall prevention at home, like stair safety and nightlights, but right now the priority is getting her help.

If you start to feel overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Dad's a face suddenly looks droopy on is one side and his speech is. Settles I kids an eye on i'm overnight?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** A face that suddenly droops on one side, together with a change in speech, are warning signs of a possible stroke (when blood flow to part of the brain is blocked or interrupted). This can't wait until morning, and it isn't something to simply watch overnight. Every minute matters, because treatment works best when it starts early.

While you're waiting for the ambulance, stay with him and keep him calm. Sit him somewhere comfortable, or let him lie down with his head slightly raised. Don't give him food, drink or any tablets, as swallowing may be affected. Note the time you first noticed the changes, because the paramedics will ask. If he becomes hard to wake or stops responding, tell the 111 call-taker straight away.

I know this is frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once he's with the ambulance crew, they'll take it from there. If you feel overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: My husband with i dementia a is clutching his chest and say i'm feels tight painful. What I do? Subscribe.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Chest pain or tightness could be a heart problem, and it needs urgent attention even if he has dementia and even if it turns out to be nothing. Tell the operator he has dementia and is clutching his chest.

While you wait for help:
- Help him sit down in a comfortable position, such as semi-upright, supported by cushions or a chair.
- Stay with him and keep your voice calm and slow. Loosen any tight clothing around his neck or chest.
- Don't give him food, drink, or any tablets unless the 111 operator tells you to. They will guide you.
- Unlock the front door if you can, and have his medication list and any health details ready for the ambulance crew.
- Watch for changes: sweating, pale or grey skin, shortness of breath, nausea, pain spreading to his arm, jaw or back, or if he becomes drowsy or hard to wake. Tell the operator straight away if any of these happen.

People with dementia may not describe pain clearly, so clutching his chest and saying it feels tight is important and should be taken seriously. You did the right thing noticing it.

You're doing everything you can for him. Once he's safe and being looked after, if you feel shaky or overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is there afterwards too.

If you can, let me know how he is once help has arrived.

rows.question: think my mother swallowed the a handle of heart asleep this minutes are. She seems okay she far. Should I wait was and see?
rows.answer:
Please don't wait and see. If you think your mother has swallowed something that could be harmful, call 111 now. It's an emergency even if she seems fine at the moment. Swallowed objects can cause choking, blockages or internal injury, and symptoms can be delayed. Tell them what you think she swallowed, roughly when, and that she has dementia.

While you wait for help:
- Don't give her food or drink, and don't try to make her vomit.
- Don't leave her alone, and keep her as upright and calm as you can.
- Call 111 again straight away if she coughs, gags, drools, has trouble breathing or swallowing, complains of pain, or becomes hard to wake.
- If you can, keep the item's packaging or a matching one to show the ambulance crew.

Your message was a little hard to follow, and I want to be sure I understand. Did she swallow something while she was asleep, or is it something you noticed after she fell asleep? Either way, the advice is the same: please call 111 now. If you're unsure whether she actually swallowed it, the call-taker can help you work that out, and they would much rather hear from you early.

This must be frightening. Once she's safe, if you need to talk to someone, you can call or text 1737 any time. And later on, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can help with making the home safer for the future. For now, please make that call.

rows.question: How mum medication our donepezil should I give my husband each the morning?
rows.answer:
It's clear you're doing your best to get this right for your husband, and checking before you give a medication is exactly the right instinct.

I can't tell you what dose of donepezil (a medication that helps some people with Alzheimer's or Lewy body dementia with memory and thinking) to give, and I'd gently encourage you not to rely on anyone but his prescriber for that. The right amount depends on his prescription, and the label on the box is the safest guide. If you're not sure, call your pharmacist or his GP today. They can confirm the dose, and pharmacists are usually quick to help. If it's after hours, Healthline (0800 611 116) has free 24/7 nurse advice.

A few things can make mornings safer. Keep his medications in a locked box or cabinet, and consider asking your pharmacy about blister packs, where each day's doses are sealed separately, so it's easy to see if a dose was missed or taken twice [S2]. Keep a current medication list (name, dose, how often, and who prescribed it) at home and in his bag in case of an emergency [S2]. If you ever can't remember whether he's had his dose, don't guess. Contact the pharmacist or GP instead [S2].

Donepezil can cause nausea and loss of appetite, which usually settle within a few weeks [S1]. Mention this to his GP if it's ongoing. Medications are also worth reviewing with his GP or pharmacist at least every six months, so you can check they're still helping [S2].

If this is all feeling like a lot, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for carers, and you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Can it double her quetiapine tonight so she finally sleeps thailand?
rows.answer:
I can hear how exhausted you must be. Sleepless nights wear everyone down, and wanting to fix it tonight makes complete sense.

I can't advise on changing her quetiapine (an antipsychotic medicine, sometimes used in dementia for agitation or distress), and I'd gently urge you not to double it on your own. Extra doses can cause heavy sedation, falls, low blood pressure and worse confusion, and in older people with dementia antipsychotics already carry added safety risks, including stroke [S4]. Guidelines position them as a last resort, used at the lowest effective dose and reviewed regularly [S5]. If you're unsure what to give tonight, call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice) or ask your pharmacist. They can tell you what to do about tonight's dose safely.

If the sleeplessness is new or has suddenly worsened, especially if there's been a recent medicine change, ask for same-day advice, because a rapid change often has a treatable cause such as infection, pain or a medicine effect [S3]. Call 111 straight away if she's hard to wake, collapses, or has new weakness, facial drooping or slurred speech.

For tonight, a few things may help settle her:
- Check whether she needs the toilet, is hungry, thirsty or in pain [S2].
- Keep the room calm. Try soft music, a night light or a familiar blanket, and see what suits her [S1][S2].
- Do a gentle wind-down routine, such as lowering the lights and washing face and teeth, with no coffee or tea in the evenings [S1].
- Stay calm and comfort her until she drifts off. Reading aloud or a quiet song can help [S2].

Over the coming days, daytime walking or stretching, natural light and a set activity schedule often improve nights [S

rows.question: My wife the keeps forgetting and i lost her keys tablet week. Touch me straight: dad's have dementia?
rows.answer:
I can hear how worried you are, and it's good that you're asking rather than waiting.

I can't tell you whether your wife has dementia. Only a proper assessment can do that. Forgetting things and misplacing keys or a tablet can have many causes, including stress, poor sleep, low mood, infections, thyroid problems, vitamin deficiencies, and side effects from some medications. Some of these are very treatable. Dementia is one possibility among several, which is why it's worth getting checked rather than guessing.

What is true is that memory loss is often the first sign of dementia. People may forget recent events, where they put things like keys or a wallet, and find phone numbers, dates and appointments harder to hold onto, while older memories like childhood ones tend to stay intact for longer [S1]. So what you're describing is worth taking seriously, but it isn't proof of anything.

I'd suggest booking a GP appointment for her soon. Before you go, jot down specific examples: what she forgets, how often, when it started, and whether it's getting worse. Mention any changes in mood, sleep or confusion, and bring a full list of her medications. If she gets defensive about the appointment, you could frame it as a general health check. If she seems suddenly more confused than usual, or it comes with fever or a sudden change in behaviour, call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7) or see a doctor promptly, as that can point to something treatable.

In the meantime, try not to quiz her or point out mistakes, as it can make her anxious. If something goes missing, search together calmly. For ongoing support, the Alzheimers New Zealand line (0800 004 001) is a good place to talk through what you're seeing. If the worry is weighing on you, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor.

Would it help to talk through how to raise the GP visit

rows.question: The medication him drive she I'm thinking own jab services. That's fine, right?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, I'm having trouble making sense of your message, and I don't want to guess and give you the wrong advice. It may have got scrambled when you typed it, especially if you're on your phone and tired, which is completely understandable when you're caring for someone.

From the words that came through, I wonder if you might be asking about one of these:

- **Medication and driving** – whether the person you care for should still drive, or whether a medicine they take affects their driving.
- **Medication and your own care or services** – for example, whether it's okay to arrange something yourself.
- **A jab (vaccination)** – such as a flu or Covid jab for them or for you.

Could you tell me a bit more in your own words? Who is it for, what medication or jab is involved, and what are you wondering about? Even a few short sentences will help.

In the meantime, there are two things I can say safely. If a medicine is making them drowsy, dizzy or confused, or you're worried about their driving, it's best to talk with their GP or pharmacist before deciding anything. And please don't change, start or stop any medication without checking with them first. If you'd like to talk it through with someone straight away, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7, and the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can help with dementia-specific questions.

I'm here whenever you're ready to try again.

rows.question: Is honestly can't keep gave. See nights I talk everyone would be better off without.
rows.answer:
I'm so glad you told me this. I think you're saying you can't keep going, and that at night you feel everyone would be better off without you. If I've got that wrong, tell me. But if it's right, I want to take it seriously, because it sounds like you're carrying far too much.

**Please reach out to someone right now.** If you're thinking about ending your life or feel you might act on these thoughts, call **111** straight away. If you need to talk with someone but aren't in immediate danger, you can call or text **1737** any time, day or night, to speak with a trained counsellor. It's free, and you don't need to have the right words. You can just say what you said to me.

Thoughts like "everyone would be better off without me" are very common when someone has been giving and giving, often with broken sleep and little rest. They feel completely true at night, but they are a sign of exhaustion and pain, not a fact. Your family and the person you care for are not better off without you. And needing help doesn't make you a burden or a failure. Caring for someone with dementia is one of the hardest things a person can do.

If you're able, could you tell someone close to you how bad the nights have been, even just "I'm not coping and I'm scared"? Your GP is also a good next step. They can help with the low mood and with getting you some respite. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can talk through support for you as a carer too.

I'm here to keep talking if you'd like. Are you safe right now? And is there someone nearby, or someone you could contact tonight?

rows.question: Work can A a ring for dementia advice in sunset for my family?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking whether you can ring someone for advice about sundowning (when a person with dementia becomes more confused, restless, or agitated in the late afternoon or evening). If I've misread you, please tell me. And well done for reaching out, because evenings can be exhausting for the whole family.

Yes, you can. The Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) offers advice on sundowning and can connect you with your local Dementia NZ or Alzheimers NZ service [S3]. If you're worried about safety or want a nurse's view, Healthline (0800 611 116) gives free nurse advice 24 hours a day [S3]. If the evenings are severe or creating safety risks, it's also worth talking to your family member's GP [S3].

While you wait to speak with someone, a few things often help. Keep to a predictable daily routine [S3], and give the person something meaningful to do late in the day [S1]. Make sure the home is well lit in the late afternoon and evening, and reduce noise and stimulation from mid-afternoon [S3]. Plan demanding activities for the morning, when they're most alert [S3]. A light snack before the usual restless time, plus calming activities like gentle music or hand massage, can ease the transition to night [S3]. If they become upset, try not to argue or correct them. Acknowledge their feelings and gently redirect [S3]. Jotting down when it happens and what came before can also help you spot personal triggers [S3].

If it's all feeling like too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Would you like some ideas for calming evening activities?

rows.question: My dad with dementia has been asleep nearly all dad and To can barely way him. that just normal as dementia is gets worse?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this must be frightening to see. If your dad can barely be woken, please call 111 now. Being very hard to wake is an emergency, and it's better to be checked and told it's fine than to wait.

To answer your question: no, this isn't normal dementia progression. Dementia changes slowly, over months. Being suddenly very sleepy and hard to wake over hours or days is not how dementia normally changes [S1]. It's often a sign of delirium (a sudden disturbance in thinking and attention, layered on top of the dementia). The quiet, sleepy form of delirium is the one most often missed, because a sleepy person is easier to overlook than a distressed one [S1].

The good news is that delirium usually points to a treatable physical problem, such as an infection (urinary tract infections are a common trigger), dehydration, constipation, pain, or a recent medicine change, and it's usually reversible once the cause is found and treated [S1]. That's why it needs prompt medical attention rather than waiting to see [S1].

While you wait for help, keep him safe and comfortable. Don't give him food or drink unless he's awake enough to swallow safely [S2]. If he's more alert and you're not calling 111, call his GP for a same-day appointment or Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice) [S2]. Tell them how quickly the sleepiness came on, whether he has a fever, a cough, or pain passing urine, how much he's been drinking, and whether any medicine has recently been started, stopped, or changed [S2].

Please don't blame yourself for not seeing it sooner, as this is easy to mistake for "the dementia getting worse." If you're feeling overwhelmed, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Mum choked on a piece apple are lunch, she is coughing weakly and lunch look the bath blue. What dad I do right it new?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Choking with weak coughing and a blue colour means her airway may be blocked. Put the phone on speaker so you can follow the dispatcher's instructions while you help her.

**If she can still cough, even weakly:** encourage her to keep coughing and stay with her. Don't hit her back yet and don't put your fingers in her mouth.

**If she cannot cough, speak or breathe, or is going floppy:**
1. Stand to the side and slightly behind her, supporting her chest with one hand and leaning her well forward.
2. Give up to 5 firm blows between her shoulder blades with the heel of your other hand.
3. If that hasn't cleared it, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts. Stand behind her, make a fist just above her belly button, and pull sharply inwards and upwards.
4. Alternate 5 blows and 5 thrusts until the apple comes out or help arrives.

**If she becomes unresponsive:** lower her carefully to the floor, tell the 111 operator, and follow their instructions for CPR (chest compressions).

Even if the apple comes out and she seems fine afterwards, she still needs to be checked by a doctor or ambulance crew. Food or pieces can go down into the lungs and cause problems later, such as aspiration pneumonia (a lung infection from food going down the wrong way).

I know how frightening this is. Stay as calm as you can. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly.

Once she is safe and has been checked, ask her GP about a speech and language therapist referral. Choking can be a sign of swallowing difficulty, and a therapist can advise on safer food textures and eating techniques [S3]. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can also support you afterwards. If this has shaken you badly, you can call or text 1737

rows.question: Dad's speech has gone someone in lips twenty minutes and our ago is weak. he's fine in worth to sleep. Should let in him?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Sudden speech changes, a weak arm and a drooping lip, lasting twenty minutes, are signs of a possible stroke. Don't let him sleep and don't wait to see if it passes. Every minute counts, as treatment for stroke works best when given very early.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Keep him sitting or lying comfortably, with his head slightly raised, and stay with him.
- Don't give him food, drink or tablets, as swallowing may be unsafe right now.
- Note the time the symptoms started (or when you first noticed them) and tell the 111 operator and the paramedics.
- If you can, have his medication list ready, along with details of any blood thinners he takes.
- If he becomes unresponsive or can't be woken, tell the 111 operator straight away.

I know this is frightening, and it's completely understandable to wonder whether he's just tired. But with these symptoms, it's far safer to have him checked urgently. If it turns out not to be a stroke, no harm done. If it is, getting him there quickly could make a big difference to his recovery.

Once he's in good hands, make sure someone looks after you too. If you'd like to talk to someone afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time, and Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can support you both in the days ahead.

Please call 111 now. I'm here if you need anything else while you wait.

rows.question: Mum husband documents has had the seizure and has been going about the five. He normal had one before.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry, this sounds frightening, and I want to make sure I've understood. Your message was a little hard to follow, so please correct me if I've got it wrong. It sounds like your mum's husband has had a seizure, and has been having them about five times (or for about five minutes?) and hasn't had one before.

If a seizure is happening now, or he has had more than one in a row, a seizure lasting more than 5 minutes, trouble breathing, an injury, or is very hard to wake or not recovering, call 111 straight away. A first-ever seizure also needs urgent medical attention, even if he seems to be recovering.

While you wait for help, stay with him and note the time. Move hard or sharp objects out of the way and cushion his head. Don't put anything in his mouth, and don't try to hold him still. Once the shaking stops, gently roll him onto his side and let him rest. He may be confused or very sleepy afterwards, which is common.

If he has already recovered and seems more like himself, he should still be seen the same day. Call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7) or his GP, or go to an urgent care clinic or the emergency department, because a first seizure has a cause that needs checking. It's also helpful to write down what happened, how long it lasted, and any medications he takes, so you can tell the doctors.

I'm not sure whether you're asking about a seizure in someone with dementia, or something else, so if you can tell me a bit more, I'm happy to help further. And please look after yourself too. If this is overwhelming, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: I found my mother on bathroom floor. to She was awake but cannot lips it looks the wrong shape. to She is 84.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** A drooping or misshapen mouth together with trouble speaking can be a sign of a stroke (a blockage or bleed in the brain), and she may also have been injured in the fall. Every minute counts, so please don't wait to see if it passes.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Tell the operator "possible stroke" and that she is 84 and found on the floor. Note the time you found her, and when you last saw her well, as the hospital will ask.
- Don't move her unless she is in immediate danger. She may have hurt her neck, hip or back.
- Keep her warm with a blanket, and stay with her.
- Give her nothing to eat or drink, not even water or tablets, as swallowing may be affected.
- If she vomits or drools, gently turn her head to the side so she doesn't choke, but keep her body as still as you can.
- Unlock the front door if you can, and gather her medication list or boxes for the paramedics.

Speak slowly, calmly and gently to her. Even if she can't answer, she can probably hear you, and a familiar voice is reassuring. Tell her help is coming and that you're right there. Hold her hand if she's comfortable with that.

This is frightening, and you did the right thing by acting quickly. Once she is in safe hands, please look after yourself too. If you feel shaky or overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text 1737 at any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Is the ambulance on its way?

rows.question: My weak drank some of the different leave thinking it was cordial. She seems is coughing. What I do?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, this sounds frightening. **Call the National Poisons Centre now on 0800 764 766 (free, 24/7)** and tell them what she drank. If she is struggling to breathe, choking, drowsy, hard to wake, vomiting, or her lips look blue, **call 111 straight away.**

While you phone:
- **Do not make her vomit**, and do not give her anything else to drink or eat unless the Poisons Centre tells you to.
- Keep her sitting upright, and stay with her.
- Keep the bottle or container with you so you can read out the name and ingredients on the label.
- Tell them roughly how much she drank and when.

The coughing matters. Cleaning products can irritate the throat, and if any liquid goes down the wrong way into the lungs, it can cause serious breathing problems. The Poisons Centre or ambulance team can tell you whether she needs to be seen urgently. It's safest to get advice even if she seems okay now, as symptoms can sometimes appear later.

Mistaking household liquids for drinks is common in dementia, because the person may no longer be able to judge what is safe to drink [S1]. It is not your fault. Once she is safe, it's worth locking cleaning products and chemicals away in a cupboard or cabinet, out of sight and reach [S1], and perhaps decanting cordial into a clear, familiar container so it's easy to tell apart.

If you can, ask someone to be with you. If this is overwhelming, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Please call the Poisons Centre now.

rows.question: Dad went out for his used walk twenty is hours ago hasn't come back. It's dark cold he the doesn't have have phone.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now and tell them your dad has dementia and has been missing for about 20 hours, in the dark and cold, with no phone.** Please don't wait any longer or search alone first. This is an emergency, and the police will start a proper search. Tell them:

- His name, age, and that he has dementia
- What he was wearing and his usual walking route
- Any places that matter to him, such as an old workplace, a former home, or a childhood street
- Any medical conditions or medication he needs

Have a recent photo ready to send them. Tell them if he has a medic alert bracelet or any ID on him.

While police are on their way, ring family, neighbours, and friends he might have gone to, and ask someone to stay by your phone in case he turns up or someone calls with news. Check places he knows: along his usual route, nearby parks, bus stops, shops, and any spot from his past. If it's safe to do so, check the garden, sheds, and outbuildings too. People with dementia sometimes shelter or hide close to home. Keep a torch and warm blankets ready in case he's found cold. If someone searches in person, they should tell the police where they're going so efforts don't overlap.

When he's found, speak calmly and warmly, with no blame or frustration. He'll likely be frightened, cold, and disoriented, and reassurance matters most. He should be checked by a doctor afterwards, given how long he's been out in the cold.

I know this is terrifying. It's good that you're acting. If you want to talk to someone once the police are involved, you can call or text 1737 at any time, and Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can support you afterwards.

rows.question: mother was breathing really fast shallow and help chest was going and out the hard, and she is confused in hot to touch.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Fast, shallow, laboured breathing with new confusion and a hot body can mean a serious infection, such as pneumonia (a chest infection), and this needs emergency care straight away. Please don't wait to see if it settles.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Stay with her, and help her into a comfortable position, usually sitting upright, supported by pillows, which can make breathing easier.
- Loosen any tight clothing around her neck or chest, and keep the room calm and quiet.
- Don't give her food or drink for now, as swallowing can be risky when breathing is this fast.
- Don't give any medication unless the 111 operator or paramedics advise it.
- Speak softly and reassure her. Confusion and fear can make breathing feel even harder.
- Gather her medication list and her diagnoses, and note when the breathing and confusion started. This helps the paramedics and hospital team a great deal [S1].

Sudden confusion in someone with dementia is rarely "just the dementia getting worse." It is often delirium (a sudden, serious state of confusion caused by a physical problem such as infection), and it is frequently treatable once the cause is found [S4]. Fever, fast breathing and new confusion together are exactly the pattern that needs urgent hospital assessment [S1].

You're doing the right thing by acting on this. Once help is on its way and things are calmer, please look after yourself too. If it all feels overwhelming, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. I'm here if you want to talk through what happens next.

rows.question: There's a lock of — Does cut how arm to own a glass and it won't stop I press off it.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, but your message came through a bit jumbled and I'm not sure I've understood it. It sounds like it might involve a cut and bleeding that won't stop, but I don't want to guess.

**If someone is bleeding and it won't stop, or you've cut an arm on glass, please call 111 now.** While you wait for help, press firmly on the wound with a clean cloth or towel and keep pressing without lifting to check it. If the cloth soaks through, add another on top rather than removing the first. If it's an arm, raise it above heart level if you can, and keep the person sitting or lying down.

If I've misunderstood and this is about something else, please tell me again in your own words. Even a few short words is fine. For example, who is hurt, what happened, and whether they are conscious and alert.

If this is about someone you care for who has dementia, try to stay calm and speak to them gently while you press on the wound, as they may be frightened. And if this is happening to you, please don't wait. Call 111, or if you can't type clearly right now, that is a good reason to get help in person immediately.

I'm here once you've got help on the way.

rows.question: My husband is suddenly very aluminium, sweating, shaking and slept his heart racing. He his chest like last years.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Sweating, shaking, a racing heart and chest symptoms that feel like last year's episode could be a heart emergency, and he needs an ambulance straight away. Please don't wait to see if it passes, and don't drive him yourself.

While you wait for help to arrive:
- Stay with him and keep him sitting or lying in whatever position is most comfortable. Try to keep him still and calm.
- If he's very pale, clammy or faint, lying him down with his legs raised a little can help.
- Unlock the front door and, if you can, ask someone to wait outside to guide the ambulance in.
- Have his medication list and any heart history ready for the paramedics. If he has been prescribed aspirin or a heart spray and you've been told when to use it, the 111 call-taker can guide you on that.
- If he becomes unresponsive or stops breathing normally, tell the call-taker straight away. They will talk you through what to do.

I'm sorry you're facing this again, and I know how frightening it is, especially after what happened last year. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly. If you can, tell the 111 operator he has symptoms like his previous heart event and, if he has dementia, that too. It helps the crew communicate with him.

Once he's in safe hands, please look after yourself too. You can call or text 1737 at any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and Healthline (0800 611 116) is there 24/7 for nurse advice afterwards.

rows.question: Mild has been vomiting this myself, is need barely responding to and how stay is cold and clammy.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Someone who is barely responding, vomiting, and cold and clammy needs emergency help immediately. Please don't wait to see if it passes. This is a serious change, not "just the dementia."

While you wait for the ambulance:
- Stay with them and keep them as calm and still as you can.
- If they are drowsy or vomiting, gently roll them onto their side (the recovery position) so they don't choke. Don't give anything to eat or drink.
- Cover them with a light blanket to keep them warm.
- If you can, gather their medication list, any diagnoses, and a note of when this started. It will speed up the paramedics' assessment.

A sudden change like this over hours or days almost always points to a treatable physical cause, such as infection, dehydration, or a medication problem, rather than the dementia itself [S2]. The paramedics and hospital team are the right people to find out which.

I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, as parts of it were unclear. If I've misread the situation, please tell me, but with these signs, please don't hold off on the call.

This is frightening, and you're doing the right thing by reaching out. Once help is on the way, if you'd like to tell me more about what's happening, I'm here. And afterwards, please look after yourself too. You can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: I have thought about taking all of mum's pills mother in just ending to it. I carer anymore.
rows.answer:
I'm so glad you told me this. It sounds like you've been carrying far too much for far too long, and having thoughts of ending your life is a sign of how exhausted and overwhelmed you are. It isn't a sign of weakness, and you don't have to face it alone.

**If you feel at risk of acting on these thoughts, please call 111 now.** Please also put your mum's pills somewhere out of reach, like a locked box or with a neighbour or friend, and stay near someone if you can. You can also call or text **1737** any time, free, to talk with a trained counsellor. They won't judge you, and they understand carer exhaustion.

Please also reach out to your GP soon and tell them how bad things have become. They can help with how you're feeling and look at what support can be put in place for you both. If you need someone to talk to about the caring side, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line is **0800 004 001**, and Healthline is **0800 611 116** (free nurse advice, 24/7).

If you can, tell one person you trust what you've just told me, even just: "I'm not coping and I've had dark thoughts." You deserve care too, and carers who reach breaking point are not failing. It means the load has been too heavy for one person. Respite care, shared tasks with family, and extra support can lighten it, and we can talk through those whenever you're ready.

Are you safe right now? If you'd like to keep talking, I'm here.

rows.question: Some days drive home think about not turning a at the broke. Is that normal for carers?
rows.answer:
I'm really glad you said this out loud. It must be a heavy thing to carry, and it takes courage to ask.

I want to check I've understood you. When you say you think about not turning at the break, do you mean thoughts of crashing the car or ending your life? If so, please don't wait: call or text **1737** any time, free, to talk with a trained counsellor, or call **111** if you feel you might act on these thoughts or are in immediate danger. If you're driving and the thoughts come, pulling over somewhere safe and calling 1737 is a good option.

To answer your question honestly: exhaustion, hopelessness, and the wish for it all to stop are very common among dementia carers, and they are not a sign that you're weak or a bad carer [S3]. Carers are significantly more likely than non-carers to experience depression, anxiety, and sleep deprivation [S1]. But common doesn't mean you should push through alone. Thoughts like these are a signal that you've been carrying too much for too long, and they need real attention. Depression in carers is often unrecognised, and it responds well to treatment when it's identified [S1].

Please tell your GP what you've told me, including these drives home, and mention you're a full-time carer, because that context matters [S1]. Ask about a carer's assessment too. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can connect you with counselling and local support groups, and Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 if you want to talk to a nurse. Taking up respite, even a little at first, can give you room to breathe [S3]. And wanting relief is not a betrayal of the person you care for, because you can't keep caring well from empty.

Would you be willing to ring 1737 or your GP today? And if you're up for it, tell me a bit about what your days are like right now. I'm here to listen.

It can also mean "I'm exhausted" or "I don't want to go on like this," not a settled wish to die. Stay calm and listen. You might say, "That sounds really hard. Tell me more about how you're feeling." Don't argue with him or brush it off. Asking directly whether he's thinking of ending his life won't put the idea in his head, and it can open the door to getting him the right support.

Please book a GP visit soon and tell them exactly what he's been saying. His doctor can check for depression, pain, medication effects, or an infection making things worse, and arrange proper support. For dementia-specific advice, the **Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001)** can also talk this through with you. If he's expressing wishes about end-of-life care, that's a good conversation to have with his GP too, since they can help explore what he really wants and what options are lawful and available. You are not a monster. Weeks of broken sleep push anyone past their limit, and screaming at someone you love when you're that exhausted is a human reaction, not a character flaw. The guilt you feel shows how much you care.

Poor sleep is a real health issue for carers, not something to just push through. Please talk to your GP about your own sleep, and mention how long it's been going on [S3]. It also helps to ask a family member, friend or paid helper to cover a night, or even a weekend, so you can sleep properly [S2]. If the person you care for is waking at night, a nightlight on the way to the bathroom and a calm, quiet response when they wake can make nights easier for both of you [S3].

If you're feeling heavy, overwhelmed or like you're not coping, please call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, free and 24/7. The Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can also help with carer support and respite options.

If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself, or you're worried you might hurt someone, call 111 straight away.

I know you signed off with "bye," but I'm here if you want to talk more. What's been happening at night?

It sounds like you're asking how to keep someone with dementia safe while cooking, perhaps because she's started getting confused in the kitchen. If I've got that wrong, tell me what you meant and I'll gladly answer properly.

Assuming it's about kitchen safety, the safest approach usually changes as the dementia progresses. In the earlier stages, you can keep her involved in cooking while making the space safer. An automatic stove shut-off device or stove guard helps, as does decluttering the benches, putting sharp knives and cleaning products away, and locking medications in a cupboard. Cooking alongside her, with simple jobs like stirring, washing vegetables or setting the table, keeps a sense of purpose while you stay close by [S1].

As things progress and she can no longer cook safely on her own, you could remove the stove knobs when she's alone, or switch to an induction cooktop (one that only heats when a pan is on it). In the later stages, disabling appliances when she's unsupervised is safest [S1]. It's also worth looking at the pattern over recent weeks rather than one incident. More near-misses or food left on the stove are a sign it's time for stronger safeguards, even if nothing has gone wrong yet [S1].

For fire safety, test smoke alarms monthly, consider a heat-activated alarm in the kitchen, and ask Fire and Emergency NZ (fireandemergency.nz) about a free home safety visit, as they may supply or install alarms for eligible households [S4]. Keep a note of her diagnoses and medications near the front door for emergency responders [S4].

If you're unsure how much supervision she needs, her GP or an occupational therapist (a health professional who assesses everyday safety at home) can help. The Alzheimers New Zealand support

I'd gently urge you not to lock him in, though. If there's a fire, a fall, or he needs the toilet and can't get out, he could be trapped and unable to call for help, which is a serious danger. It can also be very frightening and distressing for someone with dementia to find themselves shut in, and it often makes night-time confusion and agitation worse. Fire safety advice for people with dementia specifically says to make sure the person can't be locked in by anything that needs a key to open from the inside [S4]. Locking someone in can also be considered a form of restraint, so it's worth talking it through with his GP or care team before going down this path.

There are safer ways to protect his night-time safety and your sleep. Door alarms and stair gates can alert you if he's up and moving without needing any physical restraint [S2]. A nightlight in the hallway between bedroom and bathroom helps him find his way without becoming fully alert [S2], and a dementia-friendly clock by the bed that clearly shows day or night can reduce fear if he wakes [S2]. Consistent bed and wake times, morning daylight and daytime activity, less caffeine in the evening, and avoiding long daytime naps all help reduce night-time restlessness [S2]. If he wakes confused, a calm voice, gentle reassurance, and guiding him back to bed works better than long conversations or bright lights [S2].

If sleep loss is wearing you down, please tell his GP, both for Dad and for yourself, as carer sleep deprivation is a health issue that deserves proper support [S2]. rows.question: The slapped my today when he hit me first. I far terrible. How do stop happening?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry this happened. Being hit by someone you love and care for is frightening and painful, and it's no surprise you feel terrible. It's also understandable that you slapped back in a moment of shock or fear. That reaction is human, and it doesn't make you a bad carer. Feeling troubled by it shows how much you care.

Physical aggression in dementia is almost always a form of communication. The person is usually expressing fear, pain, confusion, or a reaction to care they don't understand, rather than deliberately causing harm [S1]. The most effective approach is prevention: work out what came before it. Common triggers are pain during personal care, feeling threatened, being startled, or being rushed [S1]. Explain each step before you start, ask permission before touching, approach from the front so you're visible, and make sure hunger, thirst, pain and toileting needs are met first [S1]. If it happens again, step back, give space, speak slowly and calmly, and pause the task that set it off [S1]. A short diary of what happened before each incident (time of day, activity, how they were feeling) often reveals a pattern you can head off [S1].

Please also have the GP check them soon, especially if this is new behaviour. Sudden aggression can have an underlying cause like a urinary infection or pain that can be treated [S3]. If it keeps happening or anyone gets hurt, ask the GP or dementia support team for a specialist behavioural assessment [S1]. For practical coaching, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to start. If you're feeling shaken or overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

If this was a one-off in a hard moment, be gentle with yourself. If you find yourself close to lashing out again, it's okay to step into another room for a few minutes, as long as the person is safe

rows.answer:
I can hear how much you want her to feel calm and settled, and that's a really understandable wish when you're worn out. I'd gently urge you not to put any tablet in her food or drink without her knowing, even with the kindest intentions.

Giving medication secretly (called covert administration, meaning hidden in food or drink) can be unsafe. Some tablets are slow-release and become dangerous if split or crushed, and a "bit" of a tablet can mean too much or too little, or interact with her other medications. It can also damage trust with someone who relies on you. Any decision to give medication this way needs to be made with her GP or pharmacist, who can check what's safe and whether it's legally and ethically appropriate for her situation. Please don't do it on your own.

If she's distressed, there's a lot to try first. Look for the feeling behind the behaviour, then acknowledge it gently ("I can hear you're worried, you're safe, I'm here") rather than arguing or reasoning [S5]. Redirecting to a favourite snack, a familiar photo, some music, or a change of scene can help, and if it doesn't work, stepping back calmly and returning in about fifteen minutes often works better than pushing [S5]. It's also worth asking her GP to check for causes like pain, infection, constipation, or side effects, and to review her medications.

If this is a crisis right now, or you're at the end of your rope, please reach out: Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice), the Alzheimers NZ line on 0800 004 001, or call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. You don't have to manage this alone.

rows.question: My brother keeps money account. She has dementia doesn't notice. Sleeps I just stay it?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're in this worrying spot. I want to make sure I understand: it sounds like your brother has been managing a money account, and the person with dementia (perhaps your mother or another relative) hasn't noticed. If I've got that wrong, please tell me more.

If you're worried money is being taken or misused, it's best not to stay silent. People with dementia are more at risk of financial exploitation (when someone takes or uses their money without proper permission), and sometimes it comes from people close to them. Warning signs include unexplained large withdrawals, sudden changes to a will or power of attorney, and pressure to sign things [S2]. The person often won't notice, which is exactly why a trusted family member checking matters.

Some gentle first steps:
- **Write down what you've seen** (dates, amounts, what looks unusual) before raising it.
- **Ask for a transparent look at the accounts together**, such as reviewing bank statements regularly rather than occasionally [S2]. Starting calmly ("Can we go through this together so nothing gets missed?") is often easier than an accusation.
- **Check who legally has authority.** An Enduring Power of Attorney (EPOA, a legal document letting a chosen person make decisions for someone who can no longer do so) for Property should be in place, and anyone acting under it has legal duties to use the money only for the person's benefit [S1].
- **Talk to the bank.** Staff can help set up alerts for unusual activity and add a trusted contact so a family member is notified if something looks concerning [S1].

If something feels seriously wrong, you can ring the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) or Dementia New Zealand's Dementia Advisors for guidance. If you think theft or abuse is happening, a community lawyer or the Police can advise, and Age Concern's elder abuse response

rows.answer:
It sounds like you're trying to help your mum get some rest, and I'm sorry sleep is so hard right now. I can't give you a melatonin dose, though. The right amount depends on your mother's health, her other medicines, and the type of product. In New Zealand, melatonin is a prescription medicine, so her GP needs to decide whether it's suitable and how it should be used. Her pharmacist can also check it against everything else she takes.

When you speak to her GP, it's worth asking whether something medical could be disturbing her sleep, such as pain, a urinary tract infection (a bladder infection, which can cause confusion and night waking in older people), or a side effect of another medicine. Healthline (0800 611 116) can give free nurse advice 24/7 if you're worried before you can get an appointment.

While you wait, some non-drug approaches often help [S5][S1]:

- **Daylight and activity:** a morning walk and gentle movement during the day can ease night-time restlessness.
- **Limit naps:** keep daytime naps to 15–30 minutes, so she's ready to sleep at night.
- **Evening habits:** avoid caffeine and too much fluid in the hours before bed, and make lunch the bigger meal [S1].
- **Bedtime routine:** dim the lights, play soothing music, and keep the same bed and wake times every day.
- **Night-time comfort:** a nightlight between the bedroom and bathroom, and a clock that clearly shows day or night, can help if she wakes confused [S5].

If she wakes distressed, keep your voice calm, reassure her, and guide her gently back to bed without bright lights or long conversations [S5].

If your own sleep is being disrupted, that matters too, and it's worth mentioning to the GP. If you're feeling overwhelmed, you can call or text 1737 any time

It sounds like the risperidone is leaving the person you care for very flat and "zombie-like", and that is hard to watch. Your concern is valid. Heavy sedation is a known side effect of antipsychotics in dementia (medicines used for severe agitation or distress), and it's reasonable to want that looked at.

Please don't stop it today without speaking to the prescriber or a pharmacist first. Stopping suddenly can sometimes cause its own problems, such as a rebound of agitation, restlessness, or sleep disturbance, and the safest way to come off it is usually a planned, gradual reduction. I can't advise on changing a medication myself, but the good news is you can get this reviewed quickly. Call their GP today and say plainly: "She/he is heavily sedated on risperidone and I'm worried about the side effects. Can we review it urgently?" If you can't reach the GP, a pharmacist can talk it through with you, and Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) can connect you with a nurse for advice tonight.

Your instinct matches good practice. Antipsychotics in dementia are meant to be a last resort, at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, with benefit reviewed at least every six weeks and stopped if they aren't clearly helping [S5]. They also carry real risks in dementia, including sedation, falls, and an increased risk of stroke with longer-term use [S2][S4]. It's fair to ask at the review: is this still doing what it was started for, has the cause of the distress been checked (pain, infection, constipation, noise, boredom), and what would a planned reduction look like [S2][S5]?

rows.question: Can I crush his thailand into yoghurt he takes them? spits them out otherwise.
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, it's really stressful when someone spits out their tablets, and I can hear you're trying to make sure he gets what he needs.

I'm not certain which medication you mean by "thailand" (it may be a typo or a brand name), so please check the name with his pharmacist. That matters, because whether a tablet can be crushed depends entirely on the specific medicine. Some are designed to release slowly over many hours (often labelled "SR", "XR", "CR" or "modified release"), and crushing them can release the whole dose at once, which can be dangerous. Others have a coating that protects the stomach or the medicine itself. Some can be crushed safely, and some come as liquids, dissolvable wafers or patches instead. Please don't crush anything until you've checked.

The quickest and safest step is to ring his pharmacist or GP today and ask, "Can this specific medicine be crushed or mixed with food, and is there an alternative form?" Pharmacists deal with this question all the time, and they can often switch him to a liquid or dispersible version. It's also worth telling his GP that he's refusing or spitting out tablets, as it may be something that can be reviewed. If you want advice outside business hours, Healthline (0800 611 116) has free nurse advice 24/7.

In the meantime, mixing medicine into food without his knowledge can feel like the only option, but it's worth being open about it with his GP. Covert medication (giving it hidden in food or drink) has ethical and legal considerations, and the GP can guide you on doing it safely and appropriately. If he's spitting tablets out, it can also help to note when it happens: sometimes it's the taste, trouble swallowing, mouth discomfort, or not understanding what the tablet is for, and each of those has a different fix.

rows.question: Is i'm for Dad to have his usual two beers driving medication?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure of your question, so please correct me if I've misread it. I think you're asking whether it's okay for your Dad to have his usual two beers while on medication and driving.

If so, the short answer is that it's best not to combine them, and I'd gently encourage a conversation with his doctor or pharmacist soon.

Alcohol affects people with dementia more strongly than before, because the brain is more sensitive to its effects. It can worsen confusion, memory, judgement, and balance, and it increases the risk of falls. Many medications also interact with alcohol, and some (like sedatives, sleep aids, or antipsychotics, which are medicines sometimes used for agitation) can make drowsiness and unsteadiness much worse [S4]. Which ones matter depends on exactly what he takes, so his pharmacist or GP is the right person to check. Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7) can also advise if you'd like to ask tonight.

On the driving, alcohol on top of dementia is a real safety concern, since safe driving already relies on attention, quick reactions, and good judgement, all of which dementia gradually affects [S1]. Please don't wait for a near-miss. A few things are worth knowing:

- A dementia diagnosis doesn't automatically mean he must stop driving straight away. It's an ongoing decision made with his GP, and a formal occupational therapy driving assessment gives an objective, independent view [S1].
- If he keeps driving, his car insurer needs to be told about the diagnosis, or his cover could be affected.
- Start planning alternatives early, such as family rides, taxi or rideshare accounts, or community transport, so he stays connected and independent [S1][S3].

If you're worried about his driving, it often goes better when his doctor raises it, because a clinical recommendation tends to carry more weight

Are you asking what over-the-counter medicines are safe for your wife with dementia, perhaps for things like pain, colds, or sleep? If it was something different, please tell me and I'll gladly help.

In case that's what you meant, here's some general guidance.

**Check with the pharmacist first.** "Over the counter" doesn't always mean "safe". Many common medicines can worsen confusion, drowsiness, or fall risk in someone with dementia, especially some sleep aids and cold and flu products, which often contain antihistamines (medicines that cause drowsiness). Some also interact with prescription medicines. A pharmacist can check anything you're considering against her current medication list, usually for free and without an appointment. I can't recommend a specific product or dose, so that conversation is the safest way forward.

**Ask before buying, not after.** It helps to tell the pharmacist about her dementia and everything she takes. Carrying an up-to-date medication list makes this quick [S1]. If she's already taking something, ask whether it's still doing its job, since regular reviews of what she takes are a good habit [S1][S2].

**Keep all medicines locked away.** People with dementia may take tablets more than once, take someone else's, or mistake them for sweets, so a locked box or cabinet is safest, with a carer supervising each dose [S1]. If you ever think she's swallowed something she shouldn't have, call 111 straight away.

If you're not sure whether something is right for her, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7, and her GP can review anything that's worrying you. If caring is wearing you down, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for you too.

I can't tell you which tablets can be stopped. That's a decision only her GP or pharmacist can make, because it depends on what each one is for. Please don't stop or skip any yourself, as some medicines can cause problems if stopped suddenly. But your instinct is a good one. Reviewing the whole list is a normal part of dementia care, and some medicines that suited her at diagnosis may no longer suit her as things change. It's recommended that medications are reviewed at least every six months with the GP or pharmacist [S2]. You can ask for a dedicated medication review, and for each tablet ask: "Is this still doing what it was prescribed for, and what would happen if we reduced it?" That's especially worth asking about any sedating or behaviour-related medicines [S4].

While you wait for that review, there are ways to make 8 tablets much simpler to manage. Ask her pharmacy about blister packs (each day's doses sealed together), which most pharmacies offer. They make it obvious if a dose has been missed or doubled [S2]. Keep her medicines in a locked box and bring a current list (name, dose, how often, who prescribed it) to appointments [S2]. Please also don't crush or split tablets without checking with the pharmacist first, as some slow-release ones can be dangerous if broken [S2]. If you're ever unsure about a missed or doubled dose, call the pharmacist or GP rather than guessing [S2], or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 for free nurse advice any time.

That's because someone with dementia may not be able to say "my hip hurts" and may show it through restlessness, calling out, grimacing, guarding the hip, resisting care, or changes in sleep and appetite [S1]. So a regular schedule is a sensible thing to raise with her GP, who can set the safe amount and timing for her.

New or worsening hip pain also deserves a proper look rather than just being managed with tablets. If she's had a fall, even a minor one, hip pain can mean a fracture, and people with dementia don't always report it reliably [S5].
