rows.question: Dad sees animals that anymore when he wake. me handful, is it Lot but dementia? to
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, that sounds really unsettling, and it's completely understandable that you feel overwhelmed. I'm reading your message as: Dad sees animals that aren't there when he wakes up, it's a lot to handle, and you're wondering if it's the dementia. Please tell me if I've misunderstood.

Seeing things that aren't there (hallucinations) is common in people living with dementia, so yes, it can be part of the condition. It's especially common in Lewy body dementia (a type of dementia that affects movement, alertness and memory), where seeing animals or people is often an early sign. Seeing things on waking can also happen when someone is half-asleep and confused. But I can't say what is causing it for your dad. That needs a proper assessment by his GP.

If these visions have started suddenly, or Dad also seems drowsier, more confused or more withdrawn than usual, it could be delirium (a sudden change in thinking and attention, often caused by a treatable problem like an infection, dehydration or constipation) [S1][S4]. Please see the doctor promptly in that case. It's also worth asking the GP to check his eyesight and hearing and review his medicines for side effects, since these can contribute [S1][S2]. If he is very hard to wake, call 111.

In the moment, stay calm and reassure him: "You're safe, I'm here with you." Try not to argue or insist the animals aren't there, as that tends to increase fear. His experience feels very real to him [S1]. You can also check the room for shadows or objects that could be misread, use more light and a bright night light, and keep furniture in its usual place [S1]. If the animals don't bother him, you can simply be calm alongside him. If he is frightened, gently leading him to another room can help end the vision [S1].

You're carrying a lot. Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free 24/7

rows.question: My husband is 54 and forgetting words. Does is he have early-onset dementia? need to keys before we tell kids. Bye.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry you're carrying this worry. It's frightening to notice changes in someone you love, and it makes sense that you want answers before talking to the kids.

I can't tell you whether your husband has dementia, and nobody can without a proper assessment. Word-finding trouble is common in many things, including stress, poor sleep, depression, medication side effects, thyroid problems, low vitamin B12, and infections. Some of these are fully treatable, and doctors rule them out first with blood tests, a medication review, and sometimes a brain scan [S5]. Dementia before 65 is real but less common, and it often shows up as changes in language, behaviour, or personality rather than memory loss alone [S3]. That's why word-finding difficulty is worth taking seriously.

The best next step is a GP appointment for him. It can help to jot down examples you've both noticed, when they started, whether they came on gradually or suddenly, and any new medications or big stressors. Going together is fine, and many GPs welcome it. If it turns out to be dementia, younger-onset services like YODAT (yodat.org.nz) offer support for people under 65 and their whānau [S3]. For questions along the way, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) or Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) are good places to start.

As for the kids, you don't have to tell them anything yet. Until you have answers, it's reasonable to wait, though you can say something gentle and honest if they've noticed, like "Dad's been having some trouble with words, so we're getting him checked by the doctor." Children often sense that something is off, and a simple, calm explanation usually helps more than silence.

This is a lot to hold alone. If it starts to feel overwhelming, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Would it help to talk through how to raise the G

rows.question: Can you glass a quick test I club do on mother all home two confirm has?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking whether there's a quick test you could do with your mother at home to confirm she has dementia. I'm sorry if I've misread you. It's a hard thing to be wondering about, and it's natural to want answers.

Unfortunately, there isn't a home test that can confirm dementia. Short memory quizzes found online can be unreliable, and they can also upset or embarrass someone who is already feeling uncertain. Memory changes can also have other causes that are treatable, such as infections, thyroid problems, low vitamin B12, medication side effects, depression, or poor sleep. Only a proper assessment can sort out what's going on.

What you can do at home is gather information to take to her GP. Jot down specific examples of what you've noticed: forgetting recent conversations, getting lost in familiar places, struggling with bills or cooking, mood or personality changes, and roughly when each began. If you can, bring a list of her medications too. Her GP can then do a cognitive screen and blood tests, and refer her on to a specialist if needed. This is also a good time to look at home safety, and an occupational therapist can do a room-by-room assessment on GP referral [S1].

You don't have to work through this alone. Alzheimers NZ has a free support line on 0800 004 001, and they can talk through your concerns and explain what an assessment involves [S1]. Healthline (0800 611 116) also offers free nurse advice 24/7. If worrying about your mum is weighing heavily, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

If I've misunderstood your question, please tell me more about what you're noticing with your mother and I'll do my best to help.

rows.question: Down still drive to the club twice a what. He scraped the car again. Do Was have to was anything after his licence in New Zealand?
rows.answer:
Your message came through a little jumbled, so I'm reading it as: *"Dad still drives to the club twice a week. He scraped the car again. Do we have to do anything about his licence in New Zealand?"* If I've misread, tell me and I'll adjust.

Repeated scrapes are worth taking seriously, and it's natural to feel torn when driving is tied to his independence and his club. Having a diagnosis doesn't mean he must stop driving straight away. Fitness to drive is an ongoing decision, and a formal occupational therapy (OT) driving assessment gives an objective, independent view that's more reliable than anyone's impression, including his own or yours [S1]. The best first step is to ask his GP for an appointment to discuss it. GPs in New Zealand have reporting obligations to NZTA (the transport agency) when a medical condition may affect driving safety, so the doctor can guide you on what's needed [S1]. A GP visit also takes the "bad guy" role off the family.

A few other things matter right now. Please don't secretly disable the car or take the keys without talking to him, as this tends to erode trust and cause real distress [S1]. It's usually better to say honestly that you're worried and suggest seeing the doctor together [S4]. If he keeps driving in the meantime, his car insurer needs to be told about the diagnosis, or his cover could be affected, so check that now. And start planning alternatives early: family or friends rostered for club days, community transport, or a taxi or rideshare account can keep him connected [S1][S4]. Staying involved in his community matters a great deal once driving ends.

If he is still in the early stages after diagnosis, it's also a good time to arrange Enduring Powers of Attorney (legal documents letting someone make decisions on his behalf) while he has capacity [S2]. For support with all of this, Alzhe

rows.question: I'm going and for two nights. a Mum has moderate different but she's fine in the house out own didn't to day. Can to I leave her?
rows.answer:
Some of your message came through garbled, so I may have missed details, but it sounds like you're planning to be away for two nights and wondering whether your mum, who has moderate dementia, can manage at home alone. Please correct me if I've got that wrong.

Being away overnight is a different level of risk from a few hours out, even if she copes well during the day. Moderate dementia often brings confusion at night, difficulty with meals, medications, and the stove, and trouble knowing what to do in an emergency. Most specialists would say that leaving someone with moderate dementia entirely alone for two nights isn't safe, however well she seems day to day. What she copes with while you're in the house can hide how much she's relying on you being there. That said, it depends on your mum, so a call to her GP or Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help you judge her specific situation.

The good news is there are workable options. You could have someone stay with her, a family member or trusted friend, even if it means a different person each night. If that's not possible, ask about respite care (short-term, temporary care that gives you a break), either in a rest home or through in-home support. A NASC needs assessment (the local service that works out what support she's eligible for) can help you access funded respite. Alzheimers NZ or her GP can point you towards options, and it's worth asking early, as respite can take time to arrange.

If none of that is possible this time, even a partial plan helps: a neighbour or friend dropping in morning and evening, meals prepared ahead, medications secured, and a simple way for her to reach someone. But for two full nights, a person actually staying with her is much safer than check-ins alone.

Wanting a break is completely reasonable. Carers need rest, and planning respite is part of caring well, not a failure of it. If you're feeling stretched thin, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

If

rows.question: She know leaving the gave hob on. was thinking of just turning the off at the mains programmes and letting it her use the microwave. Sensible?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you're trying to keep her safe without taking away more independence than you need to, which is a caring instinct. And yes, this is a sensible approach.

Leaving a gas hob on is a serious fire and gas risk, and you're right to act on it now. The kitchen safety guidance suggests looking at the pattern over recent weeks, not just one incident. More near-misses or forgotten food mean stronger measures are warranted, even before an accident happens [S2]. Cutting off the cooker while she's on her own, and letting her use the microwave, is a graduated step that fits with this. Taking the stove knobs off when she's alone is another common option [S2].

A few things to think through:

- **Gas supply:** If it's a gas hob, make sure the gas itself is isolated, not just the electrics. A gas isolation valve or a gas safety shut-off device is worth considering, and a gas fitter or your supplier can advise on a safe setup.
- **Microwave safety:** People with dementia can put metal, foil, or the wrong containers in a microwave, or heat things far too long. Keep it simple: a few easy-to-heat meals, clear labels, and a plain note by the microwave. Watch how she copes before assuming it's safe long term.
- **Smoke alarms:** Make sure there are working interconnected alarms, including in the kitchen, and a heat-activated one near cooking areas. Fire and Emergency NZ offers free home safety visits and may supply alarms for eligible households [S4].
- **Staying involved:** If she's still able, cooking alongside her with simple steps like stirring or washing vegetables keeps her involved and gives a sense of purpose [S2]. Easy-prepare "out of the box" options can also let her keep baking or cooking safely [S3].

If you do add technology, like a stove guard or shut-off device

rows.question: Is it okay lock Dad had a hot i bath on his own if I clammy on every 20 minutes? Bye.
rows.answer:
I can hear how much you're trying to balance Dad's independence with keeping him safe, and that's a really caring instinct. Your message is a little hard to read, so tell me if I've misunderstood, but I think you're asking whether it's okay to leave Dad in a hot bath on his own and check on him every 20 minutes.

I'd gently advise against it. The bathroom is the highest-risk room in the home for falls, and with dementia an injury may not be noticed or reported straight away [S5]. A lot can happen in 20 minutes: slipping, struggling to get out of the bath, or fainting in hot water. Hot water is a second concern, because dementia can make it hard to notice that water is dangerously hot or to react to it [S3]. It's also best not to lock the door, since he could become frightened or confused and be unable to get out, and you'd lose quick access if something went wrong.

There are ways to keep him safe while still protecting his dignity:

- Set the hot water thermostat to a maximum of 50°C, and consider anti-scald devices on the taps [S3][S5]
- Fit grab rails, a non-slip mat and a bath seat or shower chair, plus a handheld showerhead, which many people find easier and less anxious than a bath [S4][S5]
- Stay nearby, or ask whether he'd prefer you, another family member, or a support worker to help, as some people are more comfortable with one helper than another [S1]
- Keep a towel over his shoulders to maintain dignity and warmth [S1]
- Prepare everything beforehand (warm bathroom, towels and clothes at hand), explain each step simply, and try again later if he's resistant [S4]

An occupational therapist (a health professional who helps people stay safe and independent at home) can do a home assessment and recommend the right equipment for your bathroom. Your GP can refer you

rows.question: A finally said turmeric capsules reverse decisions. How many should Mum text down?
rows.answer:
It sounds like some of that message got scrambled, so I want to check I've understood you. I think you're asking about turmeric capsules and how many your mum should take, but I'm not sure what "reverse decisions" or "text down" refers to.

On the turmeric itself, I can't give a number of capsules. Dosing is for her GP or pharmacist to advise on, and that applies to supplements as well as prescription medicines. Turmeric (a yellow spice, and a common supplement ingredient) isn't a proven treatment for dementia. Studies so far haven't shown it reverses memory loss or improves decision-making. It can also interact with some medicines, especially blood thinners like warfarin, and may cause stomach upset. So please check with her GP or pharmacist before she starts, and tell them about any supplements she already takes.

If "reverse decisions" means her decision-making has been changing, that's worth raising with her GP too. Sudden changes in thinking, confusion, or judgement can sometimes have treatable causes, like infections, medication effects, or dehydration, so it's worth having them looked at. If it's something different, such as she's changing her mind a lot or you're unsure how to support her choices, tell me more and I'll gladly help. Supported decision-making (helping her choose without taking over) often works well by offering a few simple options at a good time of day [S2].

If you're keeping track of her tablets and supplements, a pharmacist-prepared blister pack and a current medication list are really useful, and a review with her GP or pharmacist at least every six months helps keep everything safe [S4].

And if you're feeling overwhelmed trying to sort all this out, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to talk it through, and Healthline (0800 611 116) can give free nurse advice any time. Could you tell me a bit more about what

rows.question: I read it available caused his Alzheimer's. Should throw out all our cookware?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you're trying to do everything you can for your loved one, and that worry makes complete sense. Your question seems to be about aluminium cookware (I'm assuming that's what you read about), so let me answer on that basis.

You don't need to throw out your cookware. The idea that aluminium pots and pans cause Alzheimer's dates back decades, but large studies since then have not found convincing evidence that cooking with aluminium causes it. Alzheimer's is understood to come from a mix of age, genetics, and other health and lifestyle factors, and no single kitchen item has been shown to be the cause. And since your loved one already has the diagnosis, replacing cookware wouldn't change its course. If the article said something different, I'm happy to help you make sense of it, and your GP can answer this too.

What does matter in the kitchen is safety. As dementia progresses, the bigger risks are forgotten food on the stove, burns, and access to chemicals. Helpful steps include a stove guard (an automatic shut-off device), removing stove knobs when the person is alone, decluttering benches, securing sharp knives, and locking cleaning products and medications in a cabinet [S1]. Locking away household chemicals is especially important, because people with dementia can lose the ability to judge what is safe to eat or drink [S2]. It's also worth checking your smoke alarms, and Fire and Emergency NZ (fireandemergency.nz) offers free home safety visits for eligible households [S4].

If you'd like to talk any of this through, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can help with kitchen adaptations and anything else on your mind. And if the worry of searching for causes or "fixes" is weighing on you, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Caring for someone you love is a lot to carry, and

rows.question: The flu jab gave my neighbour's husband donepezil. I'm letting Dad help him year?
rows.answer:
I think I'm piecing together two things here, so let me check I've understood. It sounds like your neighbour's husband takes donepezil (a medicine used for Alzheimer's and some other dementias), and you're wondering about it in relation to your dad, perhaps whether it could help him, or whether he should have a flu jab? Please correct me if I've got that wrong.

First, the flu jab and donepezil are unrelated. A flu vaccine doesn't give anyone donepezil, and donepezil is a prescription medicine, only started after a proper assessment by a GP or specialist. It's not something to pass between households or to start on someone's behalf.

If you're wondering whether donepezil might help your dad, the best step is a GP visit to talk through his symptoms. Donepezil is used for Alzheimer's disease, Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's disease dementia, but it isn't effective for vascular or frontotemporal dementia, so the type of dementia matters. Where it works, it may temporarily help memory and thinking for some people, often for around six to twelve months, but it doesn't stop or reverse the condition, and everyone responds differently [S1]. Side effects like nausea and loss of appetite are common but usually settle within a few weeks [S1]. Whether it's right for him, and at what dose, is a decision for his GP or specialist.

If your question is about the flu jab for your dad, it's generally a good idea for older people and those with health conditions, but his GP or pharmacist can confirm when and whether he's eligible.

Could you tell me a bit more about what you're hoping to sort out for your dad? And if you're feeling stretched thin looking after him, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to talk it through, and Healthline (0800 611 116) can give free nurse advice any time.

rows.question: in Thailand says injections cure vascular dementia. It $40,000. Boys it what it?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you and your family are facing this. When someone you love has dementia, a promise of a cure is very hard to ignore, and I can hear how much weight a $40,000 decision carries. I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so please tell me if I've got anything wrong.

Based on what I know, there is currently no injection or treatment anywhere in the world that cures vascular dementia (dementia caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often from strokes). Be very cautious about any clinic that claims a cure, especially one asking for large payments upfront. Some overseas clinics sell stem cell or "cell therapy" injections for dementia, and these are generally unproven, unregulated, and can carry real risks, including infection and serious complications. Please don't commit any money until a New Zealand specialist has looked at the claim.

What does help in vascular dementia is managing the underlying causes. Because it shares risk factors with heart disease (high blood pressure, diabetes, high cholesterol, smoking, inactivity), treating these is an unusually direct way to reduce the chance of further strokes and further step-downs in function [S5]. Before assuming dementia is the whole picture, it's also worth making sure treatable causes have been ruled out, such as thyroid problems, low B12, medication side effects, or infections [S2]. Structured routines, simple step-by-step tasks, and programmes like Cognitive Stimulation Therapy (group sessions of puzzles and conversation) can also help maintain thinking skills and confidence [S1].

I'd suggest talking to your GP or the person's specialist about the clinic's claims, and asking what evidence exists. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can also talk through options and local support, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice any time. If the decision is weighing on you

rows.question: Since dementia boys just normal ageing, there's point seeing the doctor the about Mum's memory, is there?
rows.answer:
I think there's a small typo in your message, so I want to make sure I'm answering what you meant. If you're asking whether dementia is just normal ageing, so there's no point seeing the doctor, the answer is the opposite: dementia is not a normal part of ageing, and it's well worth getting Mum's memory checked [S1][S4].

Some forgetfulness is part of getting older, like occasionally forgetting a name or misplacing keys but remembering later. What's different with dementia is that the changes are more persistent, get worse over time, and start to interfere with daily life, such as getting lost on a familiar route, repeating questions, struggling to find words, or becoming withdrawn or more anxious than before [S1].

There are also good practical reasons to go. Sometimes what looks like dementia is actually something treatable, such as an infection, depression, medication side effects, low vitamin levels, or a thyroid problem, and a GP can check for these [S3]. If it is dementia, an early diagnosis means earlier access to support, time to plan, and the chance for Mum to have a say in her own care [S5].

It can help to jot down what you've noticed, including examples and roughly when you first saw each change, and take that note along [S3]. If Mum is reluctant, it can feel easier to frame it as a general check-up. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can also talk through how to approach the conversation, and Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 if you're unsure whether something is urgent.

I know it's a worrying thing to be noticing in someone you love. Taking this first step is a caring thing to do, whatever the GP finds.

rows.question: My mum with is just fell the stairs and now she is need when I talk to her. What should do? Thanks for watching!
rows.answer:
**Please call 111 now.** A fall down the stairs followed by Mum being hard to rouse (or not responding when you talk to her) could mean a serious head injury, and that needs an ambulance immediately. People with dementia often can't tell you where it hurts, so don't wait to see if she improves.

While you wait for help:
- **Don't move her**, especially her head, neck or back, unless she is in immediate danger.
- **Stay with her**, keep talking calmly, and keep her warm with a blanket.
- **Don't give her food, drink or any medication.**
- **If she vomits**, becomes more drowsy, or has a seizure, tell the 111 operator straight away. If she stops breathing normally, the operator will guide you through what to do.
- **Unlock the front door** and ask someone to watch for the ambulance if you can.

I'm so sorry, this must be frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once she has been assessed and is safe, there will be time to look at stair and home safety. In New Zealand, her GP or Alzheimers NZ can help arrange an occupational therapy home assessment. [S3][S5] For now, focus only on getting her help.

If you're feeling overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text **1737** any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Dad's suddenly looks on okay and speech is slurred. I just an eye on overnight?
rows.answer:
**Please call 111 now.** Slurred speech that has come on suddenly can be a sign of a stroke, and that's an emergency. Don't wait overnight to see if it passes. Treatment works best when it's started quickly, and every minute counts.

While you wait for help, stay with him and keep him calm and comfortable, sitting up or lying on his side. Don't give him food, drink or medicines, because swallowing may be unsafe. Note the time you first noticed the change, and check for other signs like a drooping face, a weak arm or leg, or confusion. The ambulance crew will want to know all of this, and the time matters most. Have his medication list and any diagnoses ready if you can. If he becomes hard to wake or stops responding normally, tell the 111 operator straight away.

I know this is frightening, and it's not a failure on your part that it's happened. Please don't try to judge it yourself or put it down to "the dementia getting worse." A sudden change over hours is almost always something physical that needs checking and often can be treated [S1][S3]. Calling 111 is the right call, even if it turns out to be something else.

If you'd like someone to talk to once help is on the way, the 111 operator can stay on the line with you. Afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is there for you both in the days ahead.

rows.question: My husband with dementia is his chest it feels and. do die?
rows.answer:
**If your husband has chest pain, pressure, or tightness, or is struggling to breathe, please call 111 now.** Chest symptoms always need urgent checking, so please don't wait. Stay with him, help him sit or lie in whatever position is most comfortable, and keep him calm. If he's on the floor or has fallen, don't try to move him. Tell the 111 operator he has dementia, and open the door or ask someone to watch for the ambulance if you can.

I'm not sure I've understood your message, so I'm sorry if I've got this wrong. If he's saying his chest hurts and that he feels like he's going to die, that fear can be real and frightening for both of you, and people with dementia often can't describe symptoms clearly. It's safest to treat it as serious and let paramedics check him.

While you wait, speak softly and slowly, hold his hand, and let him know you're right there. Your calm presence helps more than you might realise.

Once help is on the way or you've spoken to the 111 team, please look after yourself too. This is frightening, and you shouldn't be alone with it. If it's all becoming too much, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Afterwards, Healthline (0800 611 116) or the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) can help with next steps.

If I've misunderstood and you're asking about something else, such as what the end of life looks like with dementia, tell me and I'll gently talk it through with you. But if he's unwell right now, please call 111 first.

rows.question: think my mother swallowed the a handle of heart asleep this minutes are. She seems okay she far. Should I wait was and see?
rows.answer:
Please don't wait and see. If you think your mother may have swallowed something harmful, **call 111 now**, even though she seems okay at the moment. Something swallowed can cause serious problems (like a blockage or choking) that don't show up right away, and falling asleep afterwards makes it harder to notice if she's in trouble. Tell them what you think she swallowed, roughly when, and that she has dementia.

While you wait for help:
- Keep her on her side if she's asleep or drowsy, and stay with her so you can watch her breathing.
- Don't try to make her vomit, and don't give her food or drink unless the 111 call-taker tells you to.
- Watch for coughing, gagging, drooling, trouble breathing or swallowing, pain, or any change in her colour. Tell the call-taker straight away if you see any of these.
- If you can find the object or a matching one, keep it to show the ambulance crew.

I'm sorry you're dealing with this. It's frightening, and you're right to be checking. If you're not sure what the object was, say that to the 111 operator. They'll guide you from there.

Once she's been seen and things have settled, it's worth talking with her GP about making the home safer. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can also help with practical ideas for reducing risks like this. And if you're feeling shaken afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: of give mum husband every?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, but I'm having trouble making out your question. It looks like some words may have gone missing. Could you tell me a bit more about what you'd like to ask?

If you're asking about caring for your mum or her husband (or about a husband she's caring for), I'm happy to help with things like:

- **Sharing the load** – how to ask family and friends for practical help, company, or a listening ear
- **Daily care** – routines, communication, or managing things that are difficult day to day
- **Looking after yourself** – getting breaks and support as a carer

If you're feeling overwhelmed right now, you're not alone, and that's very common in caregiving. You can call the Alzheimers New Zealand support line on 0800 004 001 to talk things through with someone who understands. If you'd like to talk to someone about how you're coping, you can also call or text 1737 any time.

Whenever you're ready, tell me what's going on and I'll do my best to help.

rows.question: Cook I double quetiapine tonight some finally sleeps through?
rows.answer:
It sounds like you're exhausted and desperate for a proper night's sleep, and that's completely understandable. But I can't advise changing the dose of quetiapine (an antipsychotic medicine sometimes used for distress or sleep problems). Please don't double it on your own. Quetiapine can cause heavy sedation, drops in blood pressure, dizziness and falls, and confusion, and people with dementia are especially sensitive to these effects. Taking extra can be dangerous, and it doesn't reliably fix sleep.

If it's late, call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice), or ask your after-hours pharmacist, and tell them what's happening overnight. Otherwise, call the GP or the prescriber first thing tomorrow and ask for an urgent review of the sleep problem and the medicine. Good guidelines advise reviewing antipsychotics regularly rather than raising them, and using non-drug approaches alongside them [S3].

If the person seems very hard to wake, is unusually drowsy, has collapsed, or you think they've had too much, call 111 straight away.

For tonight, a few things can help while you wait for medical advice:
- **Check for a physical cause.** Pain, needing the toilet, hunger, thirst, constipation or a possible infection can all disturb sleep, and sometimes meeting the need is enough to settle them [S2][S3].
- **Adjust the room.** Some people sleep better in a dark, quiet room, others with a night light and soft music. You may need to try a few things to find what works for them [S2].
- **Add comfort.** A blanket, a gentle hand massage, soothing music, or reading aloud can help them feel safe and relaxed [S2].
- **Build up the daytime.** Natural light, exercise and a regular activity routine tend to impro

rows.question: My wife keeps forgetting names looks keys them this week. swallowed: does side dementia?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're facing this. It's worrying to watch someone you love struggle with memory, and I want to make sure I understand your message, because part of it looks garbled. You mention "swallowed", so I want to check: **has your wife swallowed something she shouldn't have, such as a medication, a chemical, or a non-food item?** If so, please call **111 now**, even if she seems fine. If you can, keep the packaging or container to show the ambulance crew.

If that's not what you meant, here's what I can say about the memory changes. Forgetting names and misplacing things like keys are very common, and on their own they don't mean dementia. Everyone does it, especially when tired, stressed, or unwell. What matters is the pattern. Dementia-related changes tend to be persistent, worsen over time, and start to interfere with daily life, for example getting lost on familiar routes, struggling with familiar tasks, or repeating questions [S3].

Because you said this started "this week", the timing matters. A sudden change over days, especially with confusion, drowsiness, or acting out of character, is more often caused by something treatable, like a urinary or chest infection, dehydration, a medication change, poor sleep, or a delirium (a sudden state of confusion that needs prompt medical attention). I can't tell you the cause from here, but a sudden change is worth a GP visit soon rather than waiting. **If she has any sudden facial droop, arm weakness, slurred speech, or is hard to wake, call 111 immediately.**

You can call **Healthline on 0800 611 116** (free, 24/7) to talk it through with a nurse today. If you're worried about longer-term memory changes, book a GP appointment and jot down what you've noticed and when it began. **Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001)** can also guide you through what to expect. And if you're feeling overw

rows.question: The medication makes drowsy I'm out thinking stopping. That's fine, right?
rows.answer:
It's really understandable to want to stop something that's leaving you or your loved one feeling drowsy. That's a real quality-of-life problem, and it's worth taking seriously. But please don't stop it on your own just yet, and I can't tell you it's fine to do so.

Some medicines used in dementia care can cause problems if they're stopped suddenly, and others need a planned, gradual reduction. Which applies depends on exactly what the medicine is and why it was prescribed. Drowsiness is a very common side effect, and your GP or pharmacist may be able to adjust the plan rather than stop it outright. Reducing or stopping a medicine is actually something prescribers do regularly, but it works best when it's planned. Reviewing whether a medicine is still doing its job is a normal and encouraged part of dementia care [S3].

A few things will help. Phone your GP or pharmacist and tell them about the drowsiness; many pharmacists can give same-day advice by phone, and Healthline (0800 611 116) is free 24/7 if you want to speak to a nurse. Ask whether each medicine is still achieving its original purpose, whether the drowsiness is a known side effect, and what a safe reduction or switch might look like [S3].

One important point: if the drowsiness came on suddenly, over hours or days, rather than building gradually, or if it started after a recent medicine change, please get same-day medical advice. Sudden sleepiness can be a sign of delirium (a sudden confusion that sits on top of dementia), often from a treatable cause like an infection or dehydration [S1][S2]. And call 111 straight away if the person can't be woken, isn't responding normally, or has new weakness, facial drooping, or trouble speaking [S1].

- **How does dementia affect my family?** (relationships, roles, everyday life)
- **Who can help my family with dementia?** (support services in New Zealand)
- **How do I talk to my children or grandchildren about dementia?**

In the meantime, here is a little that may help whichever you meant. Dementia changes the whole family, not just the person diagnosed. A spouse may become a carer as well as a partner, and an adult child may find themselves making decisions for a parent who once made them for you. Many people grieve the future they had expected together, while also taking on new responsibilities [S4]. That is a lot to carry, and it's completely normal to feel overwhelmed.

You don't have to manage it alone. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) and your local Dementia NZ service can help your family find support, information and people who understand [S2]. If you're worried that someone in your family may have dementia, a good first step is a visit to their GP, who can check for treatable causes and arrange further assessment [S5]. Healthline (0800 611 116) is also free and open 24/7 if you'd like to talk something through with a nurse.

rows.question: dad dementia back asleep nearly all I become wake him. Is it just normal are dementia worse?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry, it's frightening to see your dad suddenly sleeping almost all the time. Your instinct to ask is a good one.

**If you can't wake him, he isn't responding normally, or he has new weakness, a drooping face, or trouble speaking, call 111 now.** Stay with him while you wait.

If he can be woken but is far sleepier than usual, please don't put it down to the dementia getting worse. Dementia changes slowly, over months. A sudden slide into sleeping most of the day, over hours or days, is more often a sign of delirium (a sudden change in alertness and thinking that sits on top of dementia). It can be the quiet kind, where a person is just sleepy and withdrawn rather than agitated, which is why it's so often missed [S2]. It usually points to a treatable physical cause, such as a urinary tract infection, dehydration, constipation, pain, or a recent change in medicine. Once the cause is found and treated, it's usually reversible [S2].

So this needs same-day medical advice, not watchful waiting [S3]. Please call his GP and ask for an appointment today, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7, registered nurses). It helps to tell them how quickly the sleepiness came on, whether he has a fever, pain passing urine, or a cough, how much he's been drinking, and whether any medicine was recently started, stopped, or changed [S3]. While you wait, keep him safe and comfortable, and offer fluids if he can swallow them safely [S3].

If this has crept up very slowly over many months, that's a different situation and worth raising with his GP at a routine visit. But anything sudden deserves a check today.

You're clearly looking out for him. If you're feeling worried or worn out, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor, and the Alz

rows.question: Mum choked on a piece apple are lunch, she is coughing weakly and lunch look the bath blue. What dad I do right it new?
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Your mum is choking and her lips look blue, which means she isn't getting enough air. Put your phone on speaker so the call-taker can talk you through what to do while you help her.

**Right now:**
- If she is **coughing, even weakly**, her airway is only partly blocked. Encourage her to keep coughing. Don't slap her back yet, and don't put your fingers in her mouth.
- If she **stops coughing, can't breathe or make a sound, or goes limp**, her airway is fully blocked. Lean her forward and give up to 5 firm back blows between her shoulder blades with the heel of your hand. If that doesn't clear it, give up to 5 abdominal thrusts: stand behind her, make a fist just above her belly button, and pull sharply inward and upward. Alternate between the two until the apple comes out or help arrives. The 111 operator can coach you.
- If she becomes unresponsive, lower her gently to the floor, and the operator will guide you through CPR.

**Even if the apple comes out and she seems fine,** she still needs to be checked by paramedics or in hospital. Choking can cause injury, and food or fluid that goes into the lungs can lead to a serious chest infection (aspiration pneumonia) hours or days later. Please don't give her anything to eat or drink until she has been assessed.

Once she's safe, her doctor can refer her to a speech and language therapist, who can advise on safer food textures and eating techniques. For now, though, please make the call.

You're doing the right thing by acting quickly. I'm here afterwards if you want to talk through what comes next.

- If he becomes hard to wake or stops responding normally, tell the 111 operator straight away.
- Have his medication list and any dementia diagnosis details ready to hand to the paramedics.

If you can, let a family member know so you're not on your own. This is frightening, and you're doing exactly the right thing by asking. Once he's been seen and things have settled, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can support you both, and if you're feeling overwhelmed you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor.

rows.question: My weak drank some of the different leave thinking it was cordial. She seems is coughing. What I do?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, that sounds frightening. I'm reading this as your wife (or another person you care for) drinking some cleaning liquid by mistake, thinking it was cordial, and now she is coughing.

**Call 111 now.** Swallowing a household chemical and coughing needs urgent help, even if she seems okay. Tell them exactly what she drank and roughly how much. If you can, keep the bottle or take a photo of the label so you can read out the ingredients. If you can't reach 111, the National Poisons Centre (0800 764 766, free, 24/7) can advise you straight away.

While you wait for help:
- Do not try to make her vomit, and do not give her anything to eat or drink unless the 111 call-taker or Poisons Centre tells you to. Some chemicals cause more harm coming back up.
- Sit her upright and stay with her. If she becomes drowsy, has trouble breathing, or is hard to wake, tell the call-taker straight away.
- If any got on her skin or in her eyes, rinse with plenty of clean water.
- Have her medications list and the bottle ready for the ambulance crew.

Please also be kind to yourself. This happens in many homes where someone has dementia, because the person can lose the ability to tell what is safe to drink, so it is not your fault. Once she is safe and checked, it will be worth locking all cleaning products and chemicals away in a cabinet and keeping drinks clearly separate, and your GP or Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help with ways to make the home safer.

If you feel shaken afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor. Please call 111 now, and I'm here if you need anything while you wait.

rows.question: Dad went his usual ago and hasn't come. drop and cold in he doesn't have phone.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry, this is frightening. Please act now rather than waiting. **Call 111 straight away and ask for police.** Someone with dementia who is out and not back, especially in the cold, is an emergency. Don't wait to see if he turns up.

While you're calling, have these ready:
- **A recent photo** and a description of what he's wearing
- **His usual route**, plus places that matter to him, like an old workplace, a former home, or somewhere he used to walk
- **Any health details** and medication he needs
- The time he left and how long he's been gone

If someone else is with you, ask them to check the immediate neighbourhood and his usual route while you stay by the phone. Tell neighbours or family who might spot him. Check whether he's gone to a familiar place, since people with dementia often head somewhere meaningful from their past [S2].

When he's found, stay calm and gentle and avoid blame or anger. He may be cold, scared, or confused, and warmth and reassurance matter most [S2]. Once he's home and warm, it's worth having him checked by your GP or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7) if he's been out in the cold for long.

Please call 111 now. If you can, reply and let me know when he's found. And once he's safe, I can help you with ways to make this less likely to happen again.

rows.question: My mother is really chest i gone in and out, and confused and touch.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry, this sounds frightening, and I want to make sure I've understood you. It sounds like your mother is drifting in and out of awareness, is more confused than usual, and may have chest problems.

**If she is hard to wake, unresponsive, having chest pain, struggling to breathe, or has sudden facial droop, arm weakness or slurred speech, call 111 now.** Stay with her, and if she's lying down, gently help her onto her side while you wait.

If she's not in one of those situations, this still needs to be assessed today. A sudden worsening of confusion, or going in and out of alertness, is rarely "just the dementia progressing." It very often signals a treatable physical cause, such as a chest infection or urinary tract infection, dehydration, pain, or a medication side effect. This is called delirium (a sudden state of confusion and altered alertness that can sit on top of dementia), and it's usually reversible when the cause is treated [S4]. Same-day assessment is recommended for a sudden marked increase in confusion, new fever or chills, signs of pain, or refusing food and drink for more than 24 hours [S4].

Please call her GP now for urgent advice, or ring Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice) if the surgery is closed. If you can, jot down what has changed and when, and have her medication list and diagnoses to hand. It speeds up the assessment [S4].

Your last words were cut off ("and touch"). If you meant she's hot to touch, feverish, or something else, tell me and I can help you think it through. rows.question: There's a lot blood — Dad cut arm our a glass won't stop bleeding even I press it.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Tell them your dad has a deep cut that won't stop bleeding. If you can, put the phone on speaker so you can keep both hands free.

While help is on the way:

- **Keep pressing hard** with a thick clean cloth, towel, or clothing straight onto the wound. Don't ease off to peek.
- **If blood soaks through, don't remove it.** Put more cloth on top and keep pressing.
- **Lie him down** and raise the arm above the level of his heart if you can.
- **Look for glass in the wound.** If you see any, don't pull it out. Press around it instead.
- If you have a belt or tie, you can wrap it firmly above the cut, but only if pressure alone isn't working.
- Keep him warm with a blanket, and talk to him calmly. If he seems dizzy, pale, drowsy, or confused, tell the 111 operator straight away.

The operator will guide you step by step. If you can, send someone to unlock the door or watch for the ambulance.

I know this is frightening. You're doing the right thing by pressing and getting help. Once he's safe, we can talk about anything you need, but for now, stay with him and keep pressing.

rows.question: My husband suddenly very in agitated, sweating, school says heart racing. had chest pain like last year.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Chest pain together with sweating and a racing heart can be a heart emergency, and it needs an ambulance straight away. Please don't wait to see whether it passes, and don't drive him yourself.

While you wait for help:
- Tell the 111 operator he has chest pain, sweating and a racing heart, and mention that he has dementia and has had chest pain before.
- Help him sit or lie down in a comfortable position, and stay calm and close. A quiet, steady voice will help him, because fear can make the agitation and the racing heart worse.
- Don't give him anything to eat or drink. Don't give any tablets unless the 111 operator specifically tells you to.
- If you can, unlock the front door and have his medication list and any recent hospital or GP letters ready for the ambulance crew.

It's also worth telling the crew that his agitation is new. In someone with dementia, sudden agitation can be caused by a physical problem, and here it may be linked to the chest pain, so please don't put it down to the dementia.

This is very frightening, and you're doing the right thing by acting quickly. If you can, ask a family member or neighbour to come and be with you. Once he's in safe hands and the worst has passed, please look after yourself too. You can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Mum hard been vomiting this morning, now responding to mum and skin is cold.
rows.answer:
**Call 111 now.** Vomiting followed by not responding properly and cold skin can be a medical emergency, and Mum needs help straight away. Don't wait to see if she improves.

While you wait for the ambulance:
- **Stay with her** and keep her warm with a blanket, but don't overheat her.
- **Turn her onto her side** (the recovery position, which keeps her airway clear) if she's drowsy or hard to rouse, especially if she might vomit again. Don't leave her lying flat on her back.
- **Give nothing to eat or drink**, including water or medication, until the paramedics assess her.
- Check she is breathing. The 111 operator can talk you through exactly what to do, including CPR if needed, so stay on the line and put the phone on speaker.
- If you can, gather her medication list and note when the vomiting started and what has changed. This helps the paramedics, but don't delay calling to do it.

A sudden change like this is never just "the dementia getting worse." It usually points to a treatable physical cause such as infection, dehydration, or a medication problem [S1], but it needs urgent medical assessment to find out which.

I know how frightening this is. You're doing the right thing by acting quickly. Once she's in safe hands, please look after yourself too. If you feel overwhelmed afterwards, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: Was drive home think aren't not turning. Is that normal for carers?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so please correct me if I've got it wrong. It sounds like on the drive home you noticed your thinking wasn't switching off, and you're wondering if that's normal for carers.

If that's what you meant, then yes, it's very common. Carers often describe a mind that keeps racing, replaying the day, worrying about what's next, or running through a mental to-do list, especially in quiet moments like a drive. Research shows dementia carers are far more likely than non-carers to experience sleep problems, anxiety, and low mood [S5]. Persistent fatigue and feeling unable to switch off can also be early signs of caregiver burnout, which is a predictable result of sustained caring without enough relief, not a personal failing [S4].

A few things can help. Notice which thoughts keep looping. Sometimes they're unhelpful ones, like "I have to do everything alone" or "I should not consider my own needs if I want to be a good carer" [S3]. Gently reframing them, for example "making time for myself helps me provide better care" [S2], can ease the pressure. Also try to protect sleep, get some gentle movement, and keep up connections with friends or a carer group through Carers NZ (carers.net.nz) or your local Alzheimers NZ service [S4][S5].

If your mind is racing most days, your sleep is suffering, or you're feeling persistently flat, tearful, or hopeless, please mention it to your GP and tell them you're a carer. Anxiety and depression are common in carers and respond well to treatment [S5]. You can also call the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001, or call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. If you ever feel unsafe or have thoughts of harming yourself, call 111 straight away.

I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so tell me if I've got it wrong. If you're asking whether you can text for support in the middle of the night, then yes. rows.question: safest way to my mother into your chair stops while cut?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your question, so please correct me. It sounds like you're asking how to safely help your mother from a chair, perhaps one that has stopped working or where she is stuck, and "cut" may refer to a cut or injury. If she has a significant cut, is bleeding heavily, has fallen, or may be hurt, **call 111 now** and don't try to move her yourself. Keep her still and comfortable, press a clean cloth firmly on any bleeding, and stay with her until help arrives.

If she's not hurt and you simply need to help her up from a chair safely, the key is to use her own strength rather than lifting her weight. If she can bear weight and follow simple instructions, a guided standing transfer (where you support and steer her movement instead of lifting) is much safer for both of you [S1]. Give one clear instruction at a time, such as "shuffle forward," then "lean forward," then "let's stand together," and allow plenty of time between steps [S1]. For your own back, keep your feet wide apart, your back straight, bend at the knees, and stay close to her throughout [S1]. If she starts to fall, don't try to catch her. Guide her down gently and call for help, as trying to catch someone is a leading cause of carer injury [S1].

If she can no longer bear weight safely, please don't attempt manual lifting. An occupational therapist (a health professional who assesses safe ways to move and manage daily tasks) can recommend slide sheets, transfer boards, or hoists and train you in safe handling [S1]. Your GP can refer you, or you can call Alzheimers NZ on 0800 004 001 for guidance.

rows.question: I'm I Dad his bedroom night Out sleep. He is can't work the handle. okay?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so please correct me if I've got it wrong. It sounds like you're asking whether it's okay to lock your Dad in his bedroom at night so he can't wander out while you sleep, or that he's confused by the door handle. This is a very common worry, and it comes from wanting to keep him safe and get some rest yourself.

Locking someone in their bedroom isn't something I'd recommend. If he woke up frightened, needed the toilet, or there was a fire or he had a fall, he couldn't get out and you might not get to him in time. It can also make confusion and distress worse, and it's generally considered a form of restraint, which is a serious safety and rights issue. If you're feeling at the end of your rope, that's understandable, and there are safer options.

What tends to work better is keeping him able to leave the room, while you get an alert. Door alarms or sensor mats can wake you if he gets up, and stair gates can protect the areas that worry you most [S3]. A nightlight along the hallway between his bedroom and the bathroom helps him find his way without becoming fully alert [S3]. A dementia-friendly clock that clearly shows day or night can also help him orient himself if he wakes [S3]. Check whether he needs the toilet, or is hungry, thirsty or in pain, and have his GP rule out a medical cause such as a urinary tract infection or a medication effect [S2]. During the day, daylight, a morning walk, gentle exercise and avoiding long naps can all help him sleep better at night [S3].

Broken sleep is exhausting, and your health matters too. Do speak with his GP about both his sleep and yours [S3]. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can talk through options for night-time safety and respite, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/

rows.question: I mum wife worse stay hit first. I terrible. How I stop this happening?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry. Watching your mum get worse is heartbreaking, and I can hear how much guilt you're carrying. Please hear this first: if you hit her, it doesn't make you a terrible person. It makes you an exhausted, stressed carer who reached a breaking point. Many carers have been exactly where you are, and the fact that you're asking how to stop it shows how much you care.

If you're ever worried you might seriously hurt her, or you feel out of control right now, put her somewhere safe, step away, and call 111. For free, confidential help at any time, you can call or text 1737 to talk with a trained counsellor, or call the Alzheimers NZ support line on 0800 004 001. The sooner you reach out, the better for both of you.

Now, what helps. Hitting tends to happen when stress builds up and there's no break. Here are some steps that can help:

- **Notice your warning signs.** Learn what you feel just before you lose control (a racing heart, clenched jaw, tight chest). When you feel it, step away. Even leaving the room safely for two minutes while she's safe is okay.
- **Look for what's behind her behaviour.** Her agitation or aggression is usually fear, pain, or confusion, not deliberate. Understanding what happens before a difficult moment can help you reduce or prevent it [S1]. Keeping a short diary of times, triggers, and what helped can reveal patterns.
- **Slow things down.** Explain each step of care before you start, ask permission before touching, approach from the front so she can see you, and use a calm, slow voice [S3]. Check she isn't hungry, thirsty, in pain, or needing the toilet before care tasks [S3].
- **Choose your response.** You can't control her behaviour, but you can change how you respond. A deep breath, reminding yourself she can't help it, and avo

rows.question: I pill a bend of her at tablet your tea without telling she she?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so I'll answer what I think you're asking, and please correct me if I've got it wrong. It sounds like you may be asking whether you can crush a tablet and mix it into her tea or food without telling her.

First, it's clear you're trying to look after her, and that's a hard spot to be in when she's refusing or forgetting her medication.

Please don't do this without talking to her GP or pharmacist first. Some tablets, especially slow-release ones, can become dangerous if crushed or dissolved [S3]. Hiding medication in food or drink without the person knowing is also called covert administration (giving medication secretly). It raises serious questions about consent, and it should only ever happen as a documented decision made with her doctor and pharmacist, usually with family involved, never on your own. It can also backfire. If she tastes something odd, she may start to distrust her tea and meals, and she might not finish the drink, so the dose becomes unpredictable.

There are safer things to try first. Ask the pharmacist about blister packs, where each day's doses are sealed together, so a missed or doubled dose is easy to see [S3]. Ask whether there's a liquid or dissolvable form, or whether the timing can fit more easily into her routine. Taking tablets with a favourite food, with a calm, unhurried approach, can help too. Phone her GP or pharmacist, or call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7), to talk through why she's refusing and what the options are.

If I've misunderstood, tell me a bit more about what's happening and I'll do my best to help. And if the worry of managing all this is weighing on you, you can call the Alzheimers New Zealand support line on 0800 004 001, or call or text 1737 any time to talk with a counsellor.

rows.question: My brother keeps money account. She has dementia doesn't notice. Sleeps I just stay it?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry you're dealing with this. It sounds like you're worried about the money, and I want to make sure I understand you correctly, so please correct me if I've misread.

It sounds like your brother is keeping control of the bank account of someone with dementia (perhaps your mother or another relative), and she doesn't notice while she sleeps or isn't paying attention. If that's right, you're asking whether you should simply stay quiet about it. I'd gently suggest not staying silent, because people with dementia are especially vulnerable to financial exploitation (being taken advantage of with money), and the people doing it are sometimes close family. I can't know your brother's intentions, and there may be an innocent explanation, such as him helping manage bills. But the safest approach is to make the arrangement open and legal rather than leave it unclear.

Here are some practical steps:

- **Check the legal authority.** The proper way for someone to manage her money is an Enduring Power of Attorney (EPOA, a legal document giving someone authority to act for another person) for Property. If she still has capacity to understand it, getting one in place early is the single most protective step, and it protects your brother too [S1].
- **Ask for transparency, calmly.** Suggest reviewing bank statements together as a family on a regular basis, rather than occasionally [S2]. Open, shared checking usually settles worries on both sides.
- **Add safeguards.** Account alerts for unusual activity, a trusted contact on the account, and a withdrawal limit on her card all make a real difference [S1]. Be alert to unexplained large withdrawals or pressure to change a will or power of attorney [S2].

Dementia New Zealand's Dementia Advisors and her bank's branch staff can help put these in place, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can talk through how to raise this with family. If

rows.question: milligrams melatonin can give 79-year-old mother have?
rows.answer:
I can hear that you're looking for something to help your mum sleep, and that's a really understandable thing to want when nights are hard for both of you.

I can't give a specific melatonin dose, though. The right amount depends on your mum's health, her other medicines, and how her sleep problem presents, so that's a decision for her GP or pharmacist. It's worth a quick call to either of them before giving it. In New Zealand, melatonin is generally prescription-only and not always a good fit for older people, so they'll want to check it suits her. In general terms, melatonin is a hormone your body makes to signal bedtime. Evidence that it helps sleep in people with dementia is mixed and varies from person to person, so a doctor can weigh whether it's worth trying.

While you sort that out, some non-medicine approaches can make a real difference. More daytime activity and morning daylight (a walk is ideal) help sleep at night, and so does limiting naps to 15-30 minutes [S2]. A steady bedtime routine helps too: lowering the lights, soothing music, a consistent bed and wake time [S2][S4]. Cutting back on tea, coffee and too many fluids in the evening is also worthwhile [S2]. Sleeping pills in particular can leave someone with dementia more confused or agitated [S2], which is another reason to involve her GP before adding anything.

If your mum has suddenly become unusually sleepy or her sleep has changed quickly, please get same-day advice from her GP or Healthline (0800 611 116, free 24/7). A rapid change often has a treatable cause, like an infection [S5]. And if you're not sleeping well yourself, that matters too. Tell her GP about it, and you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. The Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is also there if you'd like

rows.question: He missed morning donepezil. give him two tonight to catch out?
rows.answer:
Missing a dose is really common, and it's good that you stopped to check before doing anything. I can't advise on dosing, but please don't give two tonight just to catch up until you've spoken to a pharmacist or GP. Donepezil (a medicine that helps with memory and thinking by slowing the breakdown of a brain chemical called acetylcholine) can cause stronger side effects at higher amounts, such as nausea, vomiting, a slow heart rate or dizziness. Whether and when to take a missed dose depends on the person and the exact prescription.

The quickest way to get a clear answer is to ring your pharmacy, as they can usually answer this in a couple of minutes. Healthline (0800 611 116) also gives free nurse advice 24/7, including this late in the day. Have the medication packet or blister pack handy so you can tell them the strength and when he normally takes it.

One more thing: if he does end up having taken extra, or if he seems unusually drowsy, faint, very sick, or has a slow pulse, call 111 straight away.

You're clearly looking after his medication carefully, and one missed dose isn't a disaster. If forgotten doses keep happening, a weekly pill organiser or phone alarm can help, and your pharmacist can often set up blister packs. If it would help, I can suggest some routines to make medication times easier to remember.

rows.question: A risperidone makes mum a zombie. I'm going stop today — that's right come, isn't it?
rows.answer:
I can hear how hard it is to watch Mum so sedated, and wanting her back is completely understandable. Your instinct is a good one, but please don't stop it on your own today. Stopping it yourself isn't the right way to go about it, and I can't tell you to change a medication myself.

Risperidone (an antipsychotic, a medicine sometimes prescribed for severe distress or agitation in dementia) can cause sedation, falls and other serious risks, which is exactly why guidelines say it should be used at the lowest effective dose, for the shortest time, with regular reviews [S3][S5]. Asking for it to be reviewed or reduced is very reasonable. But stopping suddenly can sometimes bring on withdrawal effects or a return of the original distress, so the safest way is a planned reduction supervised by her prescriber. How best to do that depends on how long she's been on it and why it was started.

Please contact her GP or the prescriber today and say plainly: "Mum is very sedated on risperidone. I'd like an urgent review and a plan to reduce or stop it." If you can't reach them quickly, a pharmacist or Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7 nurse advice) can talk it through with you and advise what to do in the meantime. It's also worth asking whether each medicine is still doing its original job and whether non-drug approaches have been tried for the underlying distress [S2][S5]. These include looking for triggers like pain, constipation, infection or noise, and offering activities she enjoys.

If Mum is very hard to wake, struggling to breathe or swallow, has had a fall, or has any sudden facial droop, arm weakness or slurred speech, call 111 straight away.

You're clearly advocating for her, and that's the right thing to be doing. If it's all feeling like too much, the Alzheimers New Zealand

rows.question: Can I crush his thailand into yoghurt he takes them? spits them out otherwise.
rows.answer:
It's really stressful when he spits out his tablets, and it's good that you're thinking about how to keep him safe and comfortable.

I'm not certain which medication you mean by "thailand", so could you check the name on the pharmacy label? That matters, because some tablets must never be crushed. Slow-release or "extended-release" tablets (made to release the medicine gradually over hours) can release all their medicine at once if crushed, which can be harmful. Some others have a special coating that protects the stomach or helps absorption. Crushing a tablet that shouldn't be crushed can also change how well it works.

Please don't start crushing or hiding medication until you've checked with his pharmacist or GP. It's a quick call, and they can tell you whether that particular tablet is safe to crush. Often there's a good alternative: a liquid, dissolvable or patch form, or a different tablet that can be crushed safely. They can also look at timing and other options if swallowing or refusing tablets is becoming a pattern. If you can't reach them straight away, Healthline (0800 611 116) has free nurse advice 24/7 and can help with this too.

It's also worth letting his GP know he's refusing his medication. Refusal can have a reason behind it, such as trouble swallowing, an unpleasant taste, pain, or not understanding what the tablet is for, and sorting that out may make things easier for both of you.

If the daily battle is wearing you down, that's understandable, and you can call Alzheimers New Zealand on 0800 004 001 to talk it through with someone who knows what this is like. And if you ever feel overwhelmed yourself, you can call or text 1737 any time.

rows.question: Is it okay Dad have his used beers dementia medication?
rows.answer:
I think you're asking whether it's okay for your Dad to have his usual beers while he's on dementia medication. If I've misread that, tell me and I'll adjust.

I can't say yes or no, because it depends on which medication he's on, what else he takes, and how he's doing generally. His GP or pharmacist can give you a definite answer, and it's worth asking at his next review. They'll know his full medication list.

In general, though, alcohol and dementia don't mix well. Alcohol can add to confusion, memory problems, unsteadiness, and drowsiness, and it can make a person with dementia more likely to fall. If his medicines cause nausea, dizziness, or tiredness, alcohol may make those worse. Some other medicines, such as sedatives, sleep medicines, or antipsychotics, can interact with alcohol and increase sedation and fall risk [S2]. Dementia also changes how the brain handles alcohol, so even the amount he's always had may now affect him more than it used to.

I know this can feel like a big loss. A beer is often tied up with routine, company, and feeling like himself. If his GP agrees some alcohol is okay, ideas that sometimes help include a smaller serving, a lower-alcohol beer, having it with food, and you or another family member being around when he drinks. If the GP advises stopping, an alcohol-free beer in his usual glass can keep the ritual without the risk.

If he ever seems very drowsy, hard to wake, or very unsteady after drinking, call 111. For advice in the meantime, Healthline (0800 611 116) has free nurse advice 24/7, and Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can talk through how to handle this with your Dad. Caring for someone you love through these changes is hard, so look after yourself too. You can call or text 1737 any time if you need someone to talk to.

rows.question: What over-the-counter can back a all the chemist my wife with dementia?
rows.answer:
I'm sorry, I'm not completely sure what you're asking, so tell me if I've got it wrong. It sounds like you may be asking what over-the-counter medicines (ones you can buy at the chemist without a prescription) are safe for your wife with dementia. If you meant something different, please let me know.

If that's your question, the honest answer is that it depends on what she's taking already and what she needs it for. Many everyday products that seem harmless can cause real problems in dementia:

- **Sleep aids and some cold, flu, and allergy tablets** often contain antihistamines (drugs that cause drowsiness) that can worsen confusion and raise the risk of falls. Many people with dementia are sensitive to this.
- **Pain relief** such as paracetamol is often considered a gentler option, but the right choice and amount depend on her health and other medicines, so please check with the pharmacist rather than guessing.
- **Combination products** (like "all-in-one" cold remedies) can accidentally double up on ingredients she already takes.

The safest approach is to ask the pharmacist before buying anything. Tell them she has dementia and show them her current medicine list. Pharmacists are used to these questions and can check for interactions. It also helps to keep all medicines, including over-the-counter ones, in a locked box. People with dementia may not recognise what's safe to take, or may take something twice [S1]. If you're ever unsure about a missed or doubled dose, contact the pharmacist or GP rather than guessing [S1].

If she's unwell, in pain, or you're worried about a symptom, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7, and her GP can review everything she takes. If she has taken something harmful or is hard to wake, call 111 straight away.

What are you hoping to help her with, such as pain, sleep, or a cold?

rows.question: My mother-in-law takes 8 different tablets. Which ones car safely drop makes simpler?
rows.answer:
Managing eight tablets is a lot, and wanting to simplify things is a sensible instinct. It's a common worry for families, and it's well worth acting on.

I can't tell you which tablets are safe to drop, and please don't stop or change any of them yourselves. Some medicines can cause harm if stopped suddenly, and which ones matter most depends entirely on your mother-in-law's health. What *is* safe, and often very effective, is asking her GP or pharmacist for a full medication review. Reviewing the whole list regularly helps avoid unnecessary risk, since some medicines that suited someone at diagnosis become less suitable as dementia progresses [S1]. At the review, you can ask whether each medicine is still doing its original job, and what a planned reduction would look like. This is called deprescribing (working with the prescriber to reduce or stop medicines that are no longer helping). It's especially worth raising if any are psychotropic medicines (ones that affect mood, sleep, anxiety or behaviour), as these carry real safety risks and should be reviewed regularly rather than treated as permanent [S2].

While you wait for that appointment, you can make the day-to-day load much easier:
- Ask her pharmacy about blister packs, where each day's doses are sealed together. They make it obvious if a dose is missed or doubled [S1].
- Keep all medicines in a locked box or cabinet, and supervise doses rather than relying on memory [S1].
- Keep an up-to-date list (drug name, dose, how often, who prescribed it) at home and in her bag for emergencies [S1].
- An automatic pill dispenser with an alarm can help in early to moderate dementia, but it supplements supervision rather than replacing it [S1][S5].

It also helps to bring the whole bag of tablets to the review, including any over-the-counter medicines
