rows.answer:
I'm sorry, I'm having trouble making out your question. It looks like part of it may have been cut off or garbled, perhaps "Is four..." was meant to be a medication name or amount, and "88 45" could be a time, a weight, or an age. I don't want to guess and give you the wrong answer.

Could you tell me a bit more? For example: what medication or dose are you asking about, who it's for, and what you'd like to know.

One thing I can say: I can't confirm or advise on specific doses or how often to give pain relief, because that depends on her health, other medications, and kidney and liver function. Your GP or pharmacist is the right person to confirm this, and a pharmacist can often answer quickly over the phone. Healthline (0800 611 116) also offers free nurse advice 24/7.

In general, hip pain in someone with dementia is important to take seriously. She may not be able to say she's hurting, so pain often shows up as agitation, calling out, grimacing, guarding the hip, resisting care, or changes in sleep and appetite [S2]. Pain is often undertreated in dementia, and regular, scheduled pain relief set up with her GP can work better than only offering it when she's visibly distressed [S2].

If her hip pain is new or worsening, or if there's been a fall, she can't put weight on that leg, or she's suddenly more confused, please get her seen the same day, as a fracture or infection can be behind it [S4]. If she's had a fall with possible injury, call 111.

If you can send me the full question, I'll do my best to help. And if you're feeling stretched thin looking after her, you're welcome to call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

rows.question: herself, a drives the shops she used 30 years, cannot work TV rather. Is time is Alzheimer's?
rows.answer:
Your message came through a little jumbled, so I want to check I've understood. It sounds like someone is still driving to the shops (something she's done for 30 years), but she can't work the TV any more, and you're wondering whether it's time to consider Alzheimer's. Please correct me if I've got that wrong.

If so, that's a worrying combination, and I can see why you're asking. I can't diagnose, but I can say that struggling with a familiar, everyday task like using the TV remote, while other very familiar routines like a long-practised drive stay intact, is something GPs take seriously. It can be an early sign of changes in memory and thinking, but it can also have other causes, including infections, medication effects, vision or hearing changes, thyroid problems, low mood, or vitamin deficiencies, some of which are treatable. The next step is a proper assessment with her GP, who can check for those causes and arrange memory testing if needed. It helps to bring a short list of examples (what she's struggling with, when you first noticed it, and any getting lost or near-misses), ideally with someone who knows her well. Healthline (0800 611 116) can talk it through with you any time, and the Alzheimers New Zealand line (0800 004 001) is a good place to ask about next steps.

Because she's still driving, it's worth raising that with the GP too. Dementia doesn't mean an immediate, automatic stop; it's an ongoing decision based on assessment. Family often notice problems first, such as getting lost on familiar routes, trouble at roundabouts, or unexplained dents [S4]. A formal occupational therapy driving assessment gives an objective answer, and the GP can guide you on that. If she's diagnosed and keeps driving, her car insurer will need to be told, or her cover could be affected. It's also kind to start thinking about alternatives early, like family lifts, community transport, or a

rows.question: sees that aren't a when walks. Tell me, Lewy body dementia?
rows.answer:
Your question came through a bit jumbled, so I want to check I've understood it. I think you may be asking: *"Someone sees things that aren't there, and walks. Could this be Lewy body dementia?"* If I've got that wrong, please tell me more and I'll gladly answer again.

If so, seeing things that aren't there (visual hallucinations) is one of the most typical features of Lewy body dementia (a type of dementia that affects thinking, movement and sleep). In this type, the hallucinations are usually detailed and clear, such as seeing people, children or animals that aren't present, and they often appear early [S1]. Other common signs are confusion that swings noticeably from day to day, acting out dreams during sleep, and movement changes like slowness, stiffness or a shuffling walk [S1]. I can't say whether this is what's happening for your person, as only a proper assessment from their GP or a specialist can do that, but it's worth raising these symptoms with them.

If the person has been walking differently, such as shuffling, or has dizzy spells when standing, falls are a real risk, so it's worth mentioning to the GP too [S1]. If they walk around or leave the house, there are many reasons, including boredom, restlessness, pain, anxiety, or searching for someone or something. Keeping a simple diary of when it happens can help you spot patterns [S3].

One very important thing: people with Lewy body dementia can react badly to some antipsychotic medications, such as haloperidol, sometimes severely. So before any medication is considered for hallucinations, tell every doctor, nurse or emergency department that Lewy body dementia is suspected, and don't start or change any medication without their GP's guidance [S1].

For support, you can call Healthline on 0800 611 116 (free, 24/7 nurse advice) or the Alzheimers NZ line on 0800

rows.question: is 54 and words. Does he have early-onset dementia? I need to a know before we tell the kids.
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry you're facing this. Wanting to be sure before you tell the children is completely understandable, and it sounds like you're carrying a lot right now.

Your message seems to have been cut off, so I'm not sure what's happening with his words. Struggling to find words, or language changes more generally, can have many causes, including stress, depression, medication effects, thyroid problems, vitamin B12 deficiency, and other treatable conditions. I can't tell you whether it's dementia, and no one can without a proper assessment. What I can say is that language and personality changes (rather than memory loss) are a common first sign in some forms of younger-onset dementia, such as frontotemporal dementia (a type that affects behaviour and language), and these changes are often put down to stress or mood for months or even years before a correct diagnosis [S1][S3]. So it's worth taking seriously, and also not worth assuming the worst before he's been checked.

The next step is a GP visit. The GP will take a history, review his medications, run cognitive screening, and order blood tests to rule out treatable causes. If needed, they can refer him to a specialist such as a geriatrician, neurologist, or old age psychiatrist [S5]. It helps to go along, bring notes on what you've noticed and when it started, and tell the GP plainly that you're concerned about possible younger-onset dementia. Healthline (0800 611 116, free, 24/7) can give nurse advice in the meantime, and Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help you prepare and navigate the process, including for people under 65 [S1].

On the kids: you don't have to wait for a diagnosis to be honest with them. If they've noticed changes, it's okay to say something simple like "Dad's having trouble finding words, and we're going to the doctor to find out why." Concrete, honest language works better than vagueness,

rows.question: Can year give a quick memory test I can our my home to confirm she dementia?
rows.answer:
It's a caring instinct to want some clarity, and I can hear how much you're worried about her. But no test done at home can confirm dementia. Memory problems have many possible causes, including infections, medication side effects, low mood, poor sleep, thyroid or vitamin problems, and hearing loss, and some of these are treatable. That's why a proper assessment with her GP matters. It can rule out other causes and, if it is dementia, open the door to support sooner.

What you can do at home is notice and write down what you're seeing. Her doctor will find this very helpful. Jot down examples with rough dates, such as:

- Forgetting recent events, names or faces, or repeating the same questions
- Misplacing things and being unable to retrace her steps
- Trouble with familiar tasks like following a recipe or driving a known route
- Confusion about time or place, or difficulty finding words
- Changes in mood, personality, or withdrawing from hobbies and people [S4]

The key difference from normal ageing is that occasionally forgetting a name or misplacing something, then remembering later, is within the normal range. Dementia-related changes are more persistent, get worse over time, and start to interfere with daily life [S4]. Also note that people with dementia often keep older memories, like childhood, for longer than recent ones [S1].

If you're seeing several of these signs, book a GP appointment. If you can, go along with her and bring your notes. The GP can do a proper cognitive assessment and check for other causes. For guidance on what to expect, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) or your local Dementia NZ service (dementia.nz) can talk it through with you [S4]. Healthline (0800 611 116) is also free 24/7 if you want to speak to a nurse first.

This can be a frightening time for the whole family. If you're feeling overwhelmed, you can call

rows.question: Down still drive to the club twice a what. He scraped the car again. Do Was have to was anything after his licence in New Zealand?
rows.answer:
Your message came through a little jumbled, so I'm reading it as: your loved one, who has dementia, still drives to the club twice a week, has scraped the car again, and you're asking whether anything has to happen with his licence in New Zealand. Please tell me if I've misread. A repeated scrape is worth taking seriously, and it's a hard thing to be facing.

A dementia diagnosis doesn't mean an automatic, immediate stop to driving. It's an ongoing decision, and the usual path is through his GP. In New Zealand, GPs have obligations to tell NZTA (the NZ Transport Agency) when a medical condition may affect driving safety [S1]. The most reliable next step is to ask his GP about a formal occupational therapy driving assessment, an independent, objective check that is far more dependable than anyone's own judgement, including his [S1][S2]. If he keeps driving in the meantime, his car insurer needs to be told about the diagnosis, or his cover could be affected.

It's usually better to raise your worry honestly and kindly, and to involve his doctor, than to take the keys or quietly disable the car. Either can damage trust and cause real distress without solving the problem [S1][S4]. You might say, "I've noticed a few scrapes and I'm worried about you. Could we ask the doctor to look at it together?" Where you can, let the decision feel like his [S4].

Start planning alternatives now, especially for the club, since it's clearly important to him. That could be a family or friend driving roster, a taxi or rideshare account, or community transport, so he stays connected and doesn't become isolated if driving ends [S1][S4]. If you'd like to talk it through with someone, Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) can help with local options. And if this is weighing heavily on you, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a

rows.question: going two nights. Mum has moderate dementia she's fine in house on own my day. Can leave?
rows.answer:
Wanting a couple of nights away is completely reasonable, and it's good you're thinking it through rather than just hoping for the best. Whether it's safe really depends on your mum as an individual, so I can't give a straight yes or no. The big difference is that being fine alone during the day isn't the same as being safe alone overnight. Night is when confusion, waking disoriented, wandering, falls on the way to the toilet, and not knowing who to call are most likely. With moderate dementia, two nights alone is generally a significant risk, even for someone who copes well in daylight hours.

Some things to weigh up: Does she ever wake at night confused or try to go out? Could she manage a problem on her own, like a fall, a power cut, or a smoke alarm going off? Can she reliably use the phone? And does she recognise when something is wrong? If the answer to any of these is "not sure", that's a sign she needs someone with her.

The good news is there are alternatives. A trusted family member or friend could stay at the house, or she could stay with someone else. Respite care (short-term, planned care in a rest home or dementia unit) is designed for exactly this situation, and a NASC (Needs Assessment and Service Coordination) assessment can unlock funded respite days. A support person coming in overnight is another option to explore. Alzheimers NZ on 0800 004 001 can talk through local respite options with you, and a call to her GP is worthwhile if you're unsure about her night-time safety.

Taking a break isn't selfish. Carers who rest are better able to keep going. If you're feeling stretched thin, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

Would it help to talk through what her nights are usually like, so we can work out what kind of support would suit her best?

rows.question: keeps leaving out. thinking thailand the off at the in the microwave. Stopping?
rows.answer:
I'm having a little trouble following your message, so please tell me if I've misunderstood. It sounds like the person you care for keeps leaving something (perhaps food or a plate) in the microwave and forgetting about it, and you're asking how to stop it. If I've got that wrong, just let me know and I'll adjust.

If so, it's a very common worry, and noticing it early is a good sign. Forgetting food in the microwave, or forgetting to switch things off, is usually part of short-term memory loss rather than carelessness. The aim is to make the kitchen safer without taking away their independence all at once. A few things that help:

- **Prompts and cues:** a clear sign at the microwave ("Check: is it off? Is it empty?"), or a kitchen timer you set together so there's a sound reminder.
- **Simplify the task:** keep a limited choice of easy meals, or have ready-to-heat meals at hand, so there are fewer steps to forget.
- **Safety devices:** an automatic shut-off for the stove or appliances, and working smoke alarms that are checked regularly [S3].
- **Cook together:** doing steps like stirring or setting the table alongside them keeps them involved and gives you a natural moment to check appliances [S3].

It's also worth looking at the pattern over the last few weeks rather than one incident. If forgotten food or near-misses are becoming more frequent, that's a sign more safety measures are needed, even if nothing has gone wrong yet [S3]. As things progress, you may eventually need to limit unsupervised use of the microwave or stove, but you can take that step gradually.

It's also worth mentioning this change to their GP, as it can help guide the right level of support. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can talk through practical options with you, and Healthline (0800 611 116) is there 24/7

rows.question: the Dad have hot bath one if I 20 minutes? in
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your question. Are you asking whether it's safe for your dad to have a hot bath, or to stay in it for 20 minutes?

**If your dad has been in a hot bath and seems unwell**, such as dizzy, very drowsy, confused beyond his usual, faint, or unresponsive, please call 111 straight away and don't leave him alone.

If you're asking in general: a bath of around 20 minutes is usually fine, but with dementia the main risks are scalding and falls. Dementia can make it hard to notice that water is too hot, so please check the temperature yourself with your wrist or elbow before he gets in, and never rely on him to say if it's too hot [S3]. If possible, set your hot water thermostat to a maximum of 50°C, as at 60°C serious burns can happen within seconds [S3].

Because someone with dementia may not recognise or report an injury or feeling faint, it's safest not to leave him alone in the bath. A bath seat, non-slip mat, and grab rails help prevent falls [S5]. Have towels and clothes ready beforehand, and keep the room warm [S4]. Very hot water can also make older people dizzy when they stand, so help him get out slowly. If he becomes distressed, stop and try again later [S4].

Whether baths suit your dad's health (for example, if he has heart problems or low blood pressure) is a question for his GP. You can also call Healthline on 0800 611 116 any time for free nurse advice.

If you tell me a bit more about what happened or what you're worried about, I can give more specific guidance. And if bathtime is leaving you feeling stressed or overwhelmed, the Alzheimers NZ support line (0800 004 001) is there to help.

rows.question: A finally said turmeric capsules reverse decisions. How many should Mum text down?
rows.answer:
I think a few words got scrambled in your message, so I want to check I've understood. It sounds like someone may have suggested turmeric capsules for Mum and you're wondering how many she should take. If I've got that wrong, tell me and I'll gladly try again.

I can't give you a number of capsules, and I'd gently steer away from starting them without checking first. Supplements like turmeric (curcumin) can interact with other medicines, particularly blood thinners and some diabetes or stomach medications, and they can sometimes affect the liver. They also aren't a regulated medicine, so strength varies a lot between brands. As for the claim itself, there's no reliable evidence that turmeric reverses dementia or restores lost decision-making ability. Some research has looked at curcumin for brain health, but the results so far are uncertain and haven't shown it reverses anything. I know it's hard when someone offers hope and you're desperate to help Mum.

The safest next step is to bring the capsules, or the brand name, to Mum's GP or pharmacist and ask whether they're safe alongside her current medications. A pharmacist can check for interactions quickly, often on the spot. If you'd like to talk it through with someone, Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice 24/7, and the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can help with questions like this too.

If what you're really hoping for is a way to help Mum keep making her own decisions, there is a lot that does work. Simplifying choices (two options rather than an open question), asking at her best time of day, and giving her clear reminders can all help her stay involved in decisions for longer.

If it's been a tough stretch, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Would it help if I went through ways to support Mum's day-to-day decisions?

rows.question: I read it available caused his Alzheimer's. Should throw out all our cookware?
rows.answer:
I can hear how worried you are, and wanting to protect him is completely understandable. It sounds like you may be asking about the old idea that aluminium cookware can cause Alzheimer's (the most common type of dementia).

The short answer is that you almost certainly don't need to throw out your cookware. The aluminium theory dates back decades, but large studies since then have not shown that cooking with aluminium pots and pans causes Alzheimer's. Researchers still don't fully understand what causes it; it appears to involve a mix of age, genetics, and lifestyle and health factors, rather than one single trigger. If a particular pot is badly scratched or worn, replacing it is reasonable for general reasons, but there's no need to clear out your kitchen over this. If you've seen a specific article or claim that's worrying you, I can help you think it through.

Where the kitchen does matter for someone with dementia is safety rather than cause. Things that really make a difference include an automatic stove shut-off or stove guard, locking cleaning products and medications away (people with dementia can lose the ability to tell what's safe to eat or drink) [S2], and removing the stove knobs when he's alone if unsupervised cooking is no longer safe [S1]. It's also worth watching the pattern over recent weeks: more near-misses or forgotten food on the stove is a sign to add more safeguards, even if nothing serious has happened yet [S1]. Fire and Emergency NZ can also do a free home safety visit and may help with smoke alarms [S4].

If it would help to talk any of this through, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) can answer questions about causes and about practical home adjustments. And if you're feeling the weight of all this, you can call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor. Is there something specific you read that I can help you make sense of?

rows.question: for jab neighbour's dementia. I'm nasc out letting Dad this year?
rows.answer:
I'm not completely sure I've understood your message, so tell me if I've got this wrong. It sounds like you're asking about arranging a NASC assessment (Needs Assessment and Service Coordination, the free service that works out what funded support your Dad can get) for his dementia, possibly this year. If you meant something else, tell me and I'll gladly help.

If so, starting early is a really good idea. It usually begins with your Dad's GP, who can refer him to the local NASC service [S2]. An assessor, often a nurse, social worker, or occupational therapist, visits Dad and your whānau at home to see how much support he needs and what he's eligible for. That can include help with washing and dressing, household help, day programmes, and respite (a break for you as the carer) [S2]. Doing this before a crisis means help is in place when needs change, and if things progress you can ask for a reassessment rather than waiting [S2].

While you're waiting on the process, a few things are worth doing early. If Dad still has the capacity to make his own decisions, it's important to set up Enduring Powers of Attorney (legal documents letting someone you trust make decisions for him) for both finances and personal care and welfare, as it becomes much harder once capacity is lost [S4]. Alzheimers NZ (0800 004 001) and your local Dementia NZ service (dementia.nz) can help you work through the NASC process, find local services, and connect with other carers [S2][S3]. If you ever feel overwhelmed, you can also call or text 1737 any time to talk with a trained counsellor.

Could you clarify what you meant, especially the part about "jab" and "letting Dad this year"? Then I can give you more useful guidance.

rows.question: The clinic in Thailand says injections cure vascular dementia. $40,000. it worth?
rows.answer:
I'm so sorry you're facing this. When someone you love has dementia, a promise of a cure is incredibly tempting, and wanting to try everything is completely understandable.

Based on what's known, I'd urge real caution. There is currently no cure for dementia, including vascular dementia (dementia caused by reduced blood flow to the brain, often after strokes or small vessel damage) [S3]. Brain cells that have been damaged can't currently be restored by injections, and clinics offering this kind of treatment, often stem cell or similar "regenerative" injections, generally haven't shown their results in properly controlled, published trials. Treatments like these can also carry real risks, such as infection or reactions, on top of the cost. A guaranteed cure for $40,000 is a red flag, and it's worth asking the clinic to show you independent, peer-reviewed evidence, not just testimonials.

There are real things that can help, and they cost far less. Vascular dementia is managed by protecting the brain from further damage: controlling blood pressure, cholesterol, diabetes and heart rhythm, and following the stroke-prevention plan from your GP or specialist. Cognitive stimulation therapy, music, social activity and gentle exercise have good evidence for supporting mood and quality of life [S4]. It's also worth asking your GP to check for reversible contributors, like thyroid problems, vitamin B12 deficiency, infections or medication side effects, because treating these can sometimes improve thinking noticeably [S1].

Before spending anything or travelling, I'd suggest taking the clinic's proposal to your GP or a specialist (geriatrician or old-age psychiatrist) and asking them to review it with you. Alzheimers New Zealand (0800 004 001) can also talk it through, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse advice any

rows.question: Sort dementia boys just ageing, there's no point seeing doesn't about Mum's memory, is there?
rows.answer:
It's worth seeing the GP, even if it feels like "just getting older". Some forgetfulness is a normal part of ageing, like occasionally misplacing keys or taking a moment to find a word. Dementia is different. It's a disease of the brain, and it tends to show up as memory loss that gets in the way of daily life, such as forgetting recent events, struggling with familiar tasks, or repeating questions. In the beginning, people often forget recent things like where they put their keys or an appointment, while older memories are preserved for longer [S3]. That pattern is worth getting checked rather than putting down to age.

There's also real value in getting it looked at now. Memory problems can have other causes that are treatable, including infections, thyroid problems, low vitamin B12, depression, medication side effects, and poor sleep. A GP can check for these, and sometimes things improve once they're sorted. If it does turn out to be dementia, an early assessment means Mum can have a say in her own future, with the chance to put things like lasting power of attorney in place while she's able to, and the whole whānau can get support sooner. Early conversations about future care preferences can also protect the relationship by settling decision-making questions before they become a source of conflict [S5].

It can feel awkward to raise, and Mum may resist. It sometimes helps to frame it as a general check-up rather than "we think you have dementia", and to go along with her. It also helps to jot down specific examples of what you've noticed, so the GP has something concrete to work with. A GP visit doesn't diagnose anything on its own. It's simply the first step in finding out what's going on, and I can't tell from here whether this is ordinary ageing or something more.

If you'd like to talk it through first, the Alzheimers New Zealand support line (0800 004 001) is a good place to start, and Healthline (0800 611 116) offers free nurse adv
